8. What the three builders each do, and why there are three

All three run for every name in the index, every night. None of them is watch-list only, and none is triggered by opening a name. They are three stages of one chain, each answering a different question about a single stock.

Key. The dashed box is the whole nightly chain for one stock, repeated for every name in the index. Green boxes compute something that stays true until the chart changes. The orange box is the only one of the three that asks a question about today. At the bottom, the blue-topped box on the left is what every name gets regardless, and the orange-topped box on the right is the small set you actually read, which the swing filter chooses from what the three leave behind (see: Tonight's list is the swing filter's with improving businesses drawn first, and an evening is listed and ordered by the rule that listed it).

The arrows run one way only. The shortlist cannot be built without the ladder, and the ladder cannot be built without the bands, which is why they are three components rather than one.

8.1 The worked example

One name's figures are used throughout this document to make rules concrete. They come from a year of that name's daily bars, a large-capitalisation semiconductor company trading around 933 at the time, and they are cited later wherever a rule needs a number to be legible. The worked example illustrates the rules; it never defines them. Where a rule and the worked example disagree, the rule is right and the example is restated.

The Level builder reads sixty sessions of that stock's bars and finds the prices that matter. In the worked example those are support bands at 900 to 940, 855 to 870, 818 to 830 and 738 to 770, and resistance at 996, at 1057, at 1144 to 1214, and at the all-time high. Its output is a list of price bands, each with a role and the evidence that makes it a band. It knows nothing about buying or selling.

The Ladder builder takes those bands and turns them into a plan. The first tranche sits on the 900 to 940 band and stops on a daily close below 855, which is the low edge of the band beneath it. The second sits on 855 to 870 and stops below 815. The third sits on 818 to 830 and stops below 737. Exits scale out from 1057 upward, and the band at 996 is listed but not traded because it is closer than two typical days' moves to the blended entry, which is the mean of the first two tranche zones' midpoints and the price the position is carried at once the plan has staged what it can. None of this is about tonight; the plan holds for as long as the bands do.

The Shortlist builder is the only one of the three that asks about today. It takes the plan and tonight's close and tests six conditions. With the close at 933, the price is inside a tranche zone, which here is the first, so the reason named at entry zone fires. The next earnings date is inside the twenty-session horizon, so earnings soon fires as well. Whether the name is on tonight's list is the swing filter's answer, read through its five gates over the same plan and bands (section 11.2), and where it is, its row shows the two reasons beside the name as context (see: Tonight's list is the swing filter's with improving businesses drawn first, and an evening is listed and ordered by the rule that listed it).

Now take a name whose close sits in the middle of its range, far from every band, with no earnings near and ordinary volume. Nothing fires, and with no band holding its close the swing filter finds no setup, so it is not on the list. Its bands and its plan were still computed and stored, so opening it deliberately still shows a complete chart, a level table and a ladder. That is the difference between the two boxes at the foot of the figure: the left one is produced for all five hundred names, the right one is the handful worth reading tonight.

8.2 Why three components rather than one

The dependency runs strictly one way, and each stage has a different failure mode. A wrong band produces a wrong plan for that name. A wrong plan produces a wrong list row. A wrong condition threshold produces a list of the wrong length while every band and plan underneath it stays correct, which is a completely different thing to diagnose.

Keeping them apart is also what makes the read and write matrix in section 16 able to say anything. Each builder declares what it may touch, so a defect in the ladder cannot corrupt the bands the chart draws from, and the fixture can catch each stage on its own rather than only catching the end of the chain.

9. The level builder

Figure 9.1. How four kinds of evidence become the level summary table in the report.
Collect candidatesevery swing high and low in the window; the 20, 50 and 200-day averages; the five retracements between the last swing high and the last swing low; and every price band holding an unusually large share of the period's volume
→
Merge into bandssort by price; two candidates closer than half a typical day's move join one band, whose edges are its lowest and highest member; a chain of them wider than two typical days' moves splits at its widest gap until every part fits (see: A band is no wider than two typical days' moves, and a chain that would be wider splits at its widest gap)
→
Add toucheseach visit the price paid a band, a run of sessions whose high or low lay inside it, joins it as one touch dated the session it arrived, unless the band already holds a swing or a retracement from that visit; a touch strengthens a band and can never create one (see: A touch is one visit to a band, counted only where the band holds no swing or retracement from that visit, and it never creates a band)
Assign rolesbands above tonight's close are resistance, below are support, and the nearest on each side is marked immediate
→
Score strengthone point per member, one more for a member from the last twenty sessions, one more where a retracement and a swing coincide, one more where the band holds a heavy volume shelf
→
Levelsedges, role, strength, and every member with its date and kind

Key. A candidate is a single price with a reason to matter. Merging is what turns three prices a few points apart into one band, and half a typical day's move is the merge distance because two prices closer than that cannot be told apart by anyone trading them. That holds between neighbours and not between the ends of a chain of them, so a chain of close pairs can join prices anyone trading them tells apart, and a band is no wider than two typical days' moves: a longer chain splits at its widest gap. Touches are why a band can cite specific dated lows inside it without those days being swings in their own right. A touch is a visit rather than a session, because how long the price sat in a band is not how many times the band held it: a band the price entered, stayed in for three weeks and left has one touch, not fifteen. A visit holding a session the band already has as a swing or a retracement adds nothing, since that session is in the band once already.

The volume shelf is the addition this version makes, and it is load bearing rather than decorative. Where a large share of a period's volume changed hands in a narrow price range, many holders have that price as their cost, so they defend it on the way down and sell at breakeven on the way up. Where very little traded, there is nobody with a reason to act and price moves through quickly. A level builder without a volume profile can state neither, and both statements belong in the report. (see: Levels come from four sources: swings, moving averages, retracements of the last two swings, and heavy volume shelves)

A heavy volume shelf creates a band of its own and also adds strength to one it coincides with. The two are different questions and this document answers both: the first step collects a shelf as a candidate, so a shelf with no swing, average or retracement near it is a band on volume alone, and the last step adds a point where a band holds one. The alternative, that a shelf only ranks, would make this three sources and a modifier rather than four, and it would leave the range where almost nothing traded as something the report cannot state. (see: A heavy volume shelf creates a band of its own and also strengthens one it coincides with)

The window for swings, retracements and the volume profile is the last sixty sessions, which is about a quarter of trading and is what the worked example uses. One window and not two: a shelf drawn from a different span would put a band on volume no other member of the level table can see, and its share of the period would be a share of a different period. (see: The volume profile accumulates over the same sixty sessions as the level window) The profile divides that window's own high and low into twenty bands, and each day's volume is spread across the bands its own range covers rather than placed at its close, because a day that opened at 300 and closed at 320 did not trade every share at 320. (see: The volume profile is twenty bands across the window's own range) A name with fewer than sixty stored sessions gets no profile at all rather than one over a shorter period, since a share of the period carries no denominator on the row it is written on. (see: A name with fewer than sixty sessions gets no volume profile) Moving averages are computed from the full stored year, so the 200-day average is a real computed number rather than one copied from a data page, and they are the stated exception because an average is a price rather than a share of a period.

The five retracements are drawn between the window's most recent swing high and its most recent swing low, in whichever order they occurred. A retracement is a partial reversal of a move and so needs the two ends of one, which is one high and one low; the last two swings of any kind can be two highs, and a fraction of the distance between two highs retraces nothing. A window holding no swing of one of the two kinds produces no retracements that night rather than retracements drawn from a substitute end. (see: A retracement is drawn between the last swing high and the last swing low)

One candidate is marked differently from the others. A short moving average follows the price by construction, so a band anchored on it sits near the price whatever the price does. Measured on the worked example's own bars, the close was within half a typical day's move of its own 20-day average on seventeen of the last thirty-one sessions. Such a band is still a level and still appears on the chart, because a reader wants to see where the average sits, but each band records whether anything other than a moving average anchors it. Section 10 uses that mark.

10. The ladder builder

Figure 10.1. From the level table to the two books in the report's section 10.
Read the trend staterange: tranches on the support bands, exits on the resistance bands. uptrend: tranches on pullback bands, and the stop trails to the higher of the band beneath and the last swing low beneath the tranche. downtrend: no tranches, and the report says why rather than showing an empty table. not classified: no tranches either, because an input the rule reads is absent
→
Place tranchesup to three, one per support band whose low edge is below the price, nearest first, skipping any band anchored only by a moving average; a band straddling the price keeps its full width, since a fill can happen anywhere in it
→
Place stopseach tranche stops on a daily close below the low edge of the next support band beneath it; the whole position is invalidated on a close below the lowest band in the structure
Attach conditionseach tranche carries the pattern that makes it actionable, drawn from a fixed list: available now, a failed breakdown back into the zone, the first close back above the zone after a dip, or the second day after a shock once the first day's low has held. A tranche whose band the price has made none of these at reaches the zone, which is the absence of the four rather than a fifth pattern
→
Place exitsone per resistance band above price; a band closer than two typical days' moves is listed but not traded, because the move is inside the noise; the top of the ladder becomes a trailing rule rather than a price
→
Arithmeticrisk per tranche at the zone midpoint, reward to risk from the first tranche and from the blended first two, and the worked sizing example from a risk budget
Build the earnings tradethree setups keyed to the print: a breakout before it, a flush after it, and a gap up after it, each with a trigger, an entry, a stop and a target
→
Apply the earnings rulestate the last two prints' one-day moves and how much of the position that is, so the reader decides what to carry through the date
→
Laddersboth books, with every number and the band each came from

Key. The ladder places a position, it never sizes one. It says where to buy, where to stop, and where to sell part of what is held; how much is the reader's, and the sizing paragraph in the report is worked arithmetic from a risk budget the reader chooses. (see: Long-only share plans) (see: The plan places a position and never sizes one)

Stops are daily-close stops for a stated reason: the worked example moves about six percent on a normal day, and intraday dips through a level happen weekly, so a stop on a touch is taken out by noise while a stop on a close is taken out by a decision. Placing the stop below the next band down rather than just below the tranche follows from the same fact, because a stop closer than a typical day's move is inside the noise. (see: A tranche is a support band, and its stop is a daily close below the low edge of the next band beneath it)

A row is written for every name in the index every night, carrying the trend state and a plan that states why it is empty where it is empty (see: A ladder row is written for every index member every night). An absent plan says nothing, and the row is what lets the trend-changed condition compare tonight's label against last night's for a name that had no eligible band on either. The label itself comes from the averages and the last two swings, with a name whose long average or second swing is missing recorded as not classified with the reason rather than defaulted to a range, because the label decides whether a plan exists at all (see: The trend state is read from the averages and the last two swings, and a name that cannot be classified says so). The classifier writes nothing and hands its label to this builder, which is the single writer of the ladder row (see: The trend classifier returns its label to the ladder builder).

The trend state decides the stop, and the reason is in the literature rather than in taste. Kaminski and Lo, in the Journal of Financial Markets in 2014, show that a stop reduces expected return under a random walk and can add value where returns trend, so a single stop rule applied to both a ranging name and a trending name is wrong in one of the two cases. In a range the stop is the range floor, which is the low edge of the next support band beneath the tranche. In an uptrend it trails, to the higher of that band and the most recent swing low beneath the tranche. Taking the higher of the two rather than the swing low alone is what keeps the trailing half meaningful: read literally, trailing the last higher low puts the stop wherever that low happens to be, which on a name that has run a long way is far below the band beneath and is looser protection than the range rule gives, and a trailing stop that can sit below the range floor is not trailing anything. A stop that lands inside a support band, above its low edge and at or below its high edge, moves to that band's low edge, and again where that edge sits inside another, since a close the band still holds would end a trade the band was placed to protect; a swing low is most often a band's own member, so the stop trails where the bands leave a gap between them and sits at a band's low edge where they do not. (see: The trailing stop is the higher of the band beneath and the last swing low, and a stop inside a support band moves to that band's low edge)

Two details in the tranche rule exist for reasons worth stating. A band is eligible when its low edge is below the price, not when the whole band is, because the worked example's first tranche runs from 900 to 940 with the price at 933 inside it; a band you are already trading in is exactly the one the first tranche belongs on, and it keeps its full width because a fill can land anywhere in it. And a band anchored only by a moving average carries no tranche, because a short average tracks the price, so such a band would sit at the price about half the time and the first condition would fire on nothing having happened. The average stays on the chart; it just does not decide where to buy. (see: A moving average is a level on the chart and never an anchor for a tranche)

This rule set produces the worked example's plan exactly. Its three tranches are its three support bands, and its three stops are the low edges of the bands beneath them. Its skipped exit is the only resistance band within two typical days' moves of the entry.

The second book is keyed to dated events, of which an earnings print is one, and it never merges with the position book. (see: The second book is keyed to a dated event, and an earnings print is the only kind on file) The kinds it can carry are the kinds the calendar holds, which is what the provider files, and a dated item a research pass found is a claim with a source that reaches the report's Dates section without ever reaching this book (see: A calendar event is fetched once for the whole index, and the calendar holds provider events only).

Two things figure 10.1 names and does not specify are settled here. Each tranche's condition is decided by the band's own recent history, the four patterns tested in a stated order so exactly one matches, which is asserted in both directions rather than left to whichever fits first (see: A tranche's condition is the pattern the price has made at its own band). And each traded exit sells an equal fraction of what is held, the skipped exit taking none and the top of the ladder trailing rather than naming a price, which is scaling out of a position that already exists and so leaves the rule that the plan never sizes one untouched (see: Each traded exit sells an equal fraction of what is held, and the top of the ladder trails) (see: The plan places a position and never sizes one).

A tranche may also carry a precondition no compute component can see, such as a guide that does not imply a revenue decline. The ladder emits the tranche with its price condition and a research pass attaches the precondition with its own source, which the claim checker tests like any other claim, so nothing about whether a tranche exists depends on a paid pass having run (see: A researched precondition attaches to a tranche and never creates one).

Every figure in the three event setups is a proposal and none has been tested. Twelve numbers written as rules at a planning pass would be twelve constants nobody could later tell from measured ones, and nothing here has scored a setup yet. They are stated on the page as proposals, the way section 11 states the six reason thresholds, and they are calibrated against resolved setups on the run page rather than tuned in advance (see: The event setups' triggers are proposals until resolved setups can score them). The tranche condition lookback and its shock multiple are proposals on the same terms.

10.1 The trend rule's versions

The trend rule is the fifth ladder rule the rule version scorer replays, and three versions of it are scored beside the live rule with none of them live (see: The trend rule is a fifth ladder rule a version replays, and none of its three versions is live). Version A calls a close below both the 50-day and the 200-day average a downtrend whatever the swings say, which on 2026-09-18 reaches 129 names the live rule calls range, 86 of them carrying buying zones. Version B does the same only where the 50-day is below the 200-day, 35 names that night and 30 with zones; the 94 A adds have the 50-day at or above the 200-day. Version C removes buying zones the first night the label reads downtrend and restores them only once a new label has held for 2 nights, the 2 proposed. Stored listings keep the plan as it stood on their night. Evidence: Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) find that two-to-twelve-month losers keep underperforming, Jegadeesh (1990) and Lehmann (1990) that one-month losers reverse, George and Hwang (2004) that nearness to the 52-week high predicts returns and does not reverse, and Avramov, Kaplanski and Subrahmanyam (2021) that the distance between the 21-day and the 200-day averages predicts returns, more strongly on the long side. Each is a monthly portfolio sort and not a stop-and-target setup, so together they set a prior and not a verdict: B's names resemble intermediate-term losers, where removing buying zones is supported, and the names A adds are mostly intermediate-term winners in a sharp pullback, where momentum and short-term reversal both argue the zones may be right, which favours B. Judgement: version C's one-sided rule and its 2 nights, for which no study was found: trend labels changed on 210 of 3,523 night-to-night pairs on 2026-09-09 to 09-18 and returned the next night 35 times on 25 names, and a delay on entering downtrend would keep buying zones on a name that has just broken down.

A version is promoted only by the test a candidate faces, run on the paired difference between the version's setups and the live rule's block by block, at looks fixed when the version opens, over closed windows and on the calibrated null of section 13.6, and choosing between A and B is a comparison against the live rule as the benchmark on the same sign vectors (see: A trend version is judged by the candidates' test on its difference from the live rule). If both clear, B is kept unless A clears by 5 points, fixed before scoring. Evidence: White (2000): when the best of several is picked on the data that scores them, the right null is that the best is no better than the benchmark. Not settled by research: whether the confirmation should be 2 nights, which is read from how often a label returns and never from outcomes (the trend confirmation's nights).

10.2 Why the entry is a zone, and what the midpoint is for

A band is not a line, and the first step of a plan is not a price. The level builder reads sixty sessions of a name's bars and collects every candidate a level can come from: each swing high and low, the 20, 50 and 200-day averages, the five retracements between the last swing high and the last swing low, and every price range holding an unusually large share of the period's volume. It sorts them by price and merges, so that two candidates closer than half a typical day's move become one band whose edges are its lowest and highest member, which on the worked example is a support band running from 900 to 940. The ladder builder makes that band the first tranche because its low edge is below the price and something other than a moving average anchors it, and it keeps the band's whole width although tonight's close of 933 sits inside it, since a band the price is already trading in is exactly the band the first step belongs on. The stop is a daily close below 855, the low edge of the band beneath. The shortlist builder then asks whether tonight's close is inside a tranche zone; at 933 it is, so at entry zone fires. Every step of that chain is stated in section 9 and above in section 10, and what this subsection adds is what becomes of the zone at the point the arithmetic needs one price. Evidence: Park and Irwin (2007) review 95 modern studies of technical trading and count 56 positive, 20 negative and 19 mixed, and name data snooping, the selection of rules after the fact and the estimation of risk and transaction costs as problems most of those studies carry, so a count of positive results is not itself a finding. Not settled by research: whether a price level predicts anything at all, which is the premise the whole chain rests on and on which Osler (2000) and Chung and Bellotti (2021) already disagree (the standing of levels).

A fill can land anywhere between a band's edges, so the risk arithmetic has to be carried at one price, and the midpoint is the only price in the band that is not a choice. Risk per tranche is measured from the midpoint to the stop and reward from the midpoint to the first traded exit, which on the worked example is 65 points against 137 computed at 920, and the reward to risk on the page is that ratio. It is stated twice, from the first tranche and from the blended first two, because a plan staged across two zones is carried at neither of them alone, and the blended entry is also what the skipped exit is measured from. Judgement: the midpoint rather than the low edge, the high edge or the close. A low edge assumes the best fill the band allows and a high edge the worst, so each is a forecast of the fill wearing the clothes of arithmetic, and the midpoint is the one point in the band that asserts nothing about where the fill landed.

No record is scored from the midpoint. A setup's outcome is decided from the close of the session it was listed on, admitted only where that close sits inside the plan's own range, and the break-even stored beside the outcome is measured from that close (see: A stored break-even is measured from the close the setup was entered at, as a percentage beside the figures it is compared with) (see: An entry is admitted only inside the plan's own range, and a plan with no entry zone takes its whole range as its zone). So the figure section 13.1 states for the worked example is what its plan demanded on the evening it was drawn, and the bar a condition's record is judged against is the mean of the break-evens its own setups stored. Reading the first as the second is reading a planned figure as a measured one. Judgement: keeping the two apart rather than scoring from the midpoint, because a record scored at a price no order was ever placed at would measure how the plan was drawn instead of how it turned out.

A plan places up to three tranches rather than taking the whole position at the first, which stages a purchase instead of making it at once. Evidence: Brennan, Li and Torous (2005), over securities and dates drawn at random from CRSP between 1926 and 2003, compare the certainty equivalent of staging against buying outright for an investor with iso-elastic utility. For one who already holds the market portfolio and buys a marginal amount of a further stock, staging dominates buying outright for execution periods up to 48 months, and at 36 months the advantage runs from 5% to 134% according to risk aversion, to whether the portfolio held is value or equal weighted, and to how the added stock is drawn; where the initial portfolio is optimally levered the advantage narrows to about 3% to 6% and, on an equal weighted portfolio, disappears or reverses. For buying a diversified portfolio they find only mixed support, because a constant half in stocks and half in cash rebalanced monthly beats both. Constantinides (1979) argues the other way, that a schedule fixed in advance cannot use what later periods reveal and so is dominated by strategies that adapt to them. Judgement: what carries over and what does not. Both papers stage over calendar time, in months and in years, while the tranches here stage over price on a plan that stands for as long as the bands do; neither tests entering at a support band, and neither is a measurement of this system. What Brennan, Li and Torous reach by simulation, that transient departures of prices from fundamental value can produce the advantage they measure, is a form of the reversion a support band presumes, which is why their result is read here as a prior and never as a verdict.

The midpoint is not a forecast of where a purchase staged across the zone fills, and the error is not random. How deep into the band the purchase fills and whether the band holds are decided by the same move: a plan filled at the low edge is a plan whose level is under pressure, and one filled only near the high edge is one that turned early. The entry price and the outcome are therefore dependent, and the ratio the page states is computed as though they were not. Evidence: Linnainmaa (2010), over the exchange's order book and the investor-level records of every individual investor in Finland, finds that price-contingent orders execute selectively, and that patterns which read as behavioural, being losses around earnings announcements, weak returns after a trade and contrarian trading, arise mechanically from that selection rather than from the biases they resemble. Judgement: the direction, which is that a better fill price is bought at the cost of worse odds attached to it, and the size, which nothing read here measures over these bands. The system does not assume it away: each setup is judged against a bar simulated from its own plan under its own volatility with costs, and realized loss in multiples of planned risk is reported beside the planned figure, both of them in section 13.6.

11. The shortlist and its six reasons

Six reasons. On every evening before the swing filter's list, which 11.2 states, a name was on tonight's list if any was true, and from it the six are computed for every member every night and stand beside the filter's names as context (see: Tonight's list is the swing filter's with improving businesses drawn first, and an evening is listed and ordered by the rule that listed it). There is no score and no fixed length, because the length of the list is itself the reading: a three-name night means nothing reached a level, and a sixty-name night means the market moved through everyone's levels at once. A ranked cutoff cannot say either, since it is the same length every night. (see: Tonight's list is built from stated conditions, and a score orders it only as a rule's setting)

ReasonTrue whenWhy it is worth opening
At entry zonetonight's close is inside a tranche zonethe plan's first step is available at tonight's price
Crossed a levelthe close moved through a band edge that it was on the other side of yesterdaythe level either held or failed today, and both are decisions
Breakout on volumethe close is above a band that sat at or above last night's close, on volume above the fifty-day average (see: Breakout on volume reads resistance at the previous session's close)the one condition that argues for buying strength rather than weakness
Trend state changedtonight's label differs from last night'sthe ladder changes shape, so the whole plan is different from yesterday's
Unusual volumevolume above twice the fifty-day averagesomething happened that the price may not have shown yet
Earnings soonthe next earnings date is within twenty sessions, counted on the exchange's calendar (see: Sessions to a dated event are counted on the exchange calendar and never on stored bars)a calendar fact rather than a setup, listed so a print is never a surprise

The thresholds in the table are proposals, set before any night was measured, and none will be moved. The reasons stopped choosing tonight's list when it switched to the swing filter, and they are context on a row since so what is calibrated is how many names each of the filter's gates passes rather than how much of the index each reason fires for (see: The swing filter's shape is calibrated over its ordinary nights, a night one cause pushes past a quarter and twice its usual share is left out, and each band spans a third to three times what the ruled filter passes).

The shape clock counts, over the nights stored under the open filter version, how many members pass each gate after the market and every gate before it, the market held open, and how many reach the list. A night on which a gate counted that way, or a reason, whose own median share over every night in the window is below a quarter passes or fires for more than a quarter of the index and for more than twice that median, or on which the index's median volume is 1.8 times its fifty-day average or more, is an event night: its setups share one cause, so it is counted, marked on the run page and read by no median, and the market gate is never read for it. The quarterly expiry of 2026-09-18, when unusual volume fired on half the index and the index traded at twice its average, is the case this names. Once sixty ordinary nights are stored under one version, each gate's median count is held against its band and a shape calibration is proposed (owes: The swing filter's shape calibrated from its ordinary nights); before a version is open, no night counts toward the sixty.

The run page's Calibration region states the ordinary nights against the sixty, every event night with what made it one, each gate's median count and the list's against their bands, and each reason's share of the index as context, so the gap between the proposal and the band is visible every night and not only at sixty. Rows written before the 5.4 corrections are kept as written and drawn with a line saying so wherever a page shows them (see: Sessions to a dated event are counted on the exchange calendar and never on stored bars) (see: Breakout on volume reads resistance at the previous session's close). Earnings soon on a session before 2026-09-24 read a calendar that also held other exchanges' listings of the member's ticker, so the run page counts it toward no share, and those rows too are kept as written (see: The calendar holds each member's own listing's prints, and each night's answer replaces what its window held).

11.1 How tonight's list is chosen

On every evening before the swing filter's list, which 11.2 states, every member of the index is evaluated against the six reasons above and a name is listed when any fires; the header states the true fired count, and at most twenty rows are drawn, with every other listed name reachable from the universe screen (see: The page shows twenty and states the true count). Judgement: the twenty is what a reader can check in an evening, and the fired count carries the night's reading, since the list's length is what says whether the market moved through everyone's levels at once.

The rows are ordered by how many reasons fired, most first, then by the reward to risk the night's own plan computes from its first tranche, highest first, then by ticker in code-point order (see: Tonight's list breaks a tie in fired count by the plan's reward to risk, and a row with none is drawn after every row with one and says why). A row whose plan computes none, having no tranche, no stop on its first tranche or no traded exit, is drawn after every row with one in its fired-count group and states why in the plan's own words; on the four nights 2026-09-16 to 09-21 that was 593 of the 1,463 fired rows. The ratio is read off the plan the listing kept that night, so an earlier night is ordered by its own plans. Band strength, the highest strength of any band the night stored for the name, broke the tie before this order, and each listing records it so the order it chose is the benchmark this one is measured against. Not settled by research: whether band strength or the plan's reward to risk breaks a tie better. Chung and Bellotti (2021) find that levels with more prior bounces are more likely to bounce again, decaying with time, while Osler (2000) found the published strength ratings bore no consistent relation to bounces, the only significant differences negative (which tiebreak).

The order is measured and not assumed: three orders are compared over the twenty each would draw, fired count then band strength, the order this one replaced, as the benchmark, fired count then reward to risk, and reward to risk alone, and a switch needs a comparison over both challengers that rejects at 0.05, paired by night, with the metric and the row count fixed before any record is read (see: The order tonight's list is drawn in is compared against the order it replaces, declared before any record is read). The measure is the excess the candidates' test sums, block by block, over the setups among the twenty each order draws whose whole outcome window has closed, and it is read over the nights whose listings recorded the band strength, because bands and plans are dropped a year back and the listing is kept; no comparison is drawn until every order holds the floor of blocks (see: A listing records the band strength the old order read, and the three orders are compared over the nights that recorded it). Judgement: the strength is recorded on the listing rather than each order's draws, because the draws can be rebuilt from the fired count, the strength and the plan the row keeps. Evidence: White (2000) on testing the best of several against a benchmark, and Diebold (2015) on paired loss differentials with dependence-robust errors. Hansen (2005)'s test for superior predictive ability is known here only from secondary sources.

Three facts the reasons read and the table above does not state: a plan holds at most 3 tranches, nearest the close first; the tranche a reason names is the nearest; and the fifty-day volume average includes the night's own volume, so volume above twice it is about 2.04 times the mean of the forty-nine sessions before. Judgement: each has been what the code does since the ladder and the shortlist were built, and a rule a reader cannot find is a rule a reader cannot check.

Three candidate conditions are evaluated beside the six every night, for every member, in shadow, and none reaches a screen until it is promoted on its record; they are registered by one command at one instant, so each is judged at a third of the level (see: The three candidates are registered at one instant). Arrived and narrow: the previous close was above the nearest buying zone, tonight's close is inside it, and the zone is no wider than 1 typical daily move, the 1 proposed; a close from above the zone to below it fell through the zone and is not an arrival (see: A price that has come down into a narrow buying zone since the previous session is a candidate condition). Evidence: Osler (2000) scores a level by whether the price arrives at it and reverses; Chung and Bellotti (2021) find a level's prior bounces and age bear on whether it holds, so each verdict records the band's strength and the sessions since its newest member, untested; Kavajecz and Odders-White (2004) find levels coincide with depth on the limit order book. Judgement: the width of 1 typical move: no study sets it, and at 1 the candidate would have fired 2 to 14 times a night over the nine stored nights.

Volume against the night: tonight's volume over its fifty-day average is above 2 and above 2 times the night's median ratio, the median taken before any name is evaluated over the members with a fifty-day average and some volume tonight, recorded on every verdict, and computed with no request (see: Unusual volume measured against the night's own median is a candidate condition). Evidence: Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin (2001) class a day as high volume by its rank in the stock's own fifty-day window and find the effect holds when a day is ranked by the stock's share of market volume, which controls for a market-wide day, so each verdict records the rank of tonight's volume in its window; Campbell and Wasley (1996) measure abnormal volume against a market-adjusted expectation. Judgement: the multiple 2, which has no research basis; on the nine stored nights the candidate differs from the live reason only on 2026-09-18, 18 against 252.

Crossed by a margin: the close sits at least 0.5 of a typical daily move past the edge it crossed, the high edge on a rise and the low edge on a fall, the 0.5 settled by the operator on 2026-09-22 over counts re-derived from the nine stored nights, where it fires 18 to 46 names a night against 38 to 89 at 0.25 and 112 to 176 for the live reason (see: A crossing is a candidate condition only where the close sits half a typical move past the edge it crossed). Not settled by research: the margin; Osler (2003) finds stop-loss orders cluster just beyond round numbers and rates move rapidly once they cross them, which bears on what follows a crossing and not on how far past it counts (the crossing margin).

Every threshold phase 10 chose was chosen on per-night counts, with no forward return and no setup outcome read, which is what keeps three an accurate count of what was tried (see: Nothing a candidate or a version is registered with changes while it runs, and a proposed number is settled only by a new registration). Evidence: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) show that significance hurdles must rise with how much was tried, and Sullivan, Timmermann and White (1999) that simple technical rules on the DJIA and the S&P 500 lose their apparent profit once the rules tried are counted.

11.2 Tonight's list from the swing filter

From the first night the swing filter's step records its session, tonight's list is the names the filter passes. Every member of the index is read through five gates in order, the market, the name's trend and relative strength, a setup, a trigger and a trade, and a name passing all five that no exclusion removes is listed (see: Tonight's list is the swing filter's with improving businesses drawn first, and an evening is listed and ordered by the rule that listed it). The market gate reads the night's breadth against its floor, and a night below it lists nobody. The trend and strength gate asks for an uptrend and a relative strength at or above its floor. The setup is a pullback into an anchored support band from the high of the last 20 sessions, on volume that dried up while it came down, and it is the one setup the filter reads: a tight base breaking out through a band on volume was measured over eight years at about five names a year, too few for the loop ever to judge, and was removed, to return only as a registered candidate (see: The swing filter reads pullbacks alone, and a breakout returns only as a registered candidate built from its measured record). The trigger is the pullback's event arriving, its first happening within the arrival window read off the stored gate results of the sessions before (see: Arrival is a trigger that first fired within the last three sessions, and the trade is read from tonight's close). The sessions before the filter's first stored night hold no results of their own, and theirs can be replayed and stored for the arrival alone and taken out once no night can read them (see: The swing filter's results are replayed for the sessions before its first stored night for the trigger's arrival alone, and removed once no night can read them). The trade gate reads the plan the open filter version names: the ladder's first tranche; the swing trade at the nearest bands, entered at tonight's close with its stop at the setup band's low edge and its target at the nearest band above; or section 10's plan for the swing trade, entered at tonight's close with its stop at the setup band's low edge, or at the low edge of the next support band beneath it where the setup band's is less than a typical day's move below the entry, and its target at the lowest band two typical days' moves or more above, the plan the live filter reads (see: The swing filter's trade gate reads section 10's plan for the swing trade, and the plan at the nearest bands is the variant in the reward to risk variant's place). It asks for a reward to risk at or above its floor with the stop between its two distances in typical moves. The exclusions are earnings inside the holding window, a suspect series and a gap. Section 17 states every threshold, and the filter version holding them is named on every row.

The names passing are ordered first by the state the night's readings of their reported quarters give them, improving first, then steady, then the members reading no state, being not enough quarters and no fundamentals yet, then deteriorating, and within a state by the trade's reward to risk, higher first, then relative strength, then the setup band's strength, then the ticker, each a fact about the chart, the plan or the company's reported quarters and none an opinion about the company (see: A page ranks no company as an investment, and the one reading of a company that orders a list is the direction of its reported quarters). The state orders the names the gates passed and removes none, since no gate reads it (see: Four readings of a member's reported quarters are worked out every night by rules the measured split settled, and its state is read from sales and operating margin alone). The order is applied where the list is read, tonight's page, the overnight queue, the night's own request and Past picks, by one rule over the night's stored readings, and a night that stored none, which is every night before the first that did, keeps the filter's own order wherever it is drawn (see: Tonight's list is the swing filter's with improving businesses drawn first, and an evening is listed and ordered by the rule that listed it). At most twenty are drawn and the true count is stated (see: The page shows twenty and states the true count); the ruled filter passed a median of three names a night over the stored year, so the list will rarely approach twenty, and that is the filter's selectivity rather than a fault. A night the market gate closed draws no row and one line with the breadth and its floor, and a night no name passed draws one line with how many reached each gate, so an empty list says why it is empty. The six reasons are still computed for every member every night and stored on its listing row, and on the filter's list they stand beside each name as context and choose nothing.

An evening is listed by the rule that listed it. The night records its session as the filter's once the filter has stored its rows, before any later step can stop the night, and an evening the store holds no such record for was listed by any of the six reasons firing, which is every evening before the switch, drawn in the order 11.1 states. Every surface that says whether a name was on the list reads each evening by its own rule and names it: tonight's list and its header, a name's page, its listing history and its walk, the universe's last evening and strip, the run page's overlap, the facts retention, the overnight queue and the night's own request. The run page states how many of the night's names were on the list the evening before and at least once over the five and the twenty evenings before.

11.3 A worked example

Five figures follow the swing filter through one night and one name. The first three are drawn from what the code computes over the committed fixture, the fixture's date in each key, and a check regenerates them from the fixture and holds this section to them word for word; the last two are illustrative, say so, and state no figure a limit, a decision or a claim rests on (see: Tonight's list is the swing filter's with improving businesses drawn first, and an evening is listed and ordered by the rule that listed it).

Key. Computed by the swing filter over the committed fixture's 4 members on 2026-09-04, at section 17's proposed values with no filter version open. Each bar is how many members passed that gate and every gate before it, and the figure at the right is how many that gate removed; the last bar is the names no exclusion removed, which is the list.

A night is read from the top down: where the bars drop is where the night's names stopped, and an empty bar says no name got further, so the list is empty for a reason the figure names.

Key. Computed over the committed fixture on 2026-09-04 at section 17's proposed values. No member passed every gate that night, so the figure draws the one that passed the most, KEYS, and names the first gate that stopped it. The green band is the anchored support band the setup read, the dashed green line the stop at its low edge, the orange line the target at the nearest resistance band above the close, and the dotted line the highest high of the last 20 sessions the pullback is measured from. The plan is the swing trade at the nearest bands: entered at the night's close, stopped below the band, won at the target. Section 10's plan, which the live trade gate reads, places the same stop and target for KEYS that night.

Every figure on the plan is a fact about the chart: where support sits, how far the price came down to it, and what the trade stands to gain against what it risks. None of it is a forecast, and a name that fails a gate is not on the list however good its plan looks.

Key. Replayed by the code over the committed fixture as of 2026-07-31, an earlier session than the fixture's nights, so the closes after it are stored and the setup can resolve: the latest session at least twenty sessions before the fixture's night at which a member passed the setup gate and its swing plan resolved, at section 17's proposed values. The dot on the left is the entry at that session's close, the dashed green line the stop and the orange line the target; the ringed close is the one that decided it, the first close past either line.

A setup is scored on closes and on nothing else: a close through the stop is a loss and a close at the target is a win, whichever comes first, and one that reaches neither inside 63 sessions is unresolved and never a win.

Key. Illustrative: the positions show the order the events come in and not when they fall. The upper lane is the shape clock, which counts ordinary nights under one filter version and proposes a setting for your ruling, and is frozen after the one further acceptance the bound allows. The lower lane is the edge clock, which reads each candidate's blocks and can first retire one at its first look and first promote one at the look after.

Nothing on the edge clock moves a threshold before its looks, and nothing on the shape clock reads an outcome, which is why the list can be tuned early and judged only late.

Key. Illustrative, with invented shares. Each bar is one group's share of setups that reached target before stop, and the orange mark is the break-even its own plans demanded. The first group is what the filter admitted; each other is what one gate or one exclusion alone kept out while everything else passed; a group below the block floor draws no bar.

A gate is earning its place where the setups it alone rejects fall short of their own break-even, and costing setups where they clear it. Each group is a population and not a test, so it says where to look and never moves a threshold by itself.

11.4 The setup families

The page is drawn from setup families and not from one rule. A family is a rule of its own: it reads every member every night, passes the names its gates pass in its own order, and keeps its own picks, variants, record and checkpoints (see: Tonight's page is drawn from setup families, each a rule of its own listing at most five a night). The swing families share the night's machinery. One market check, the swing filter's, is read by every swing family, so a night it closes lists nobody under any of them, and the sector heavyweights read none (see: The market check closes every swing family's list together, and the sector heavyweights read none). One open trade rule holds a stock to one trade across every swing family, and one page lists the swing families in its order, the order they are stated in below, each family's names in that family's own order up to the count section 17 states, a stock two families pass once, under the first of them with a place left, carrying the other's label, and the sector heavyweights' card after them keeps its own one holding a stock (see: A stock holds one trade across every swing family, and one qualifying under two is listed once under the first in the page's order). A family's record counts every trade its own rule passed, the ones the page gave to another family among them, so one family's change moves no other family's record; the one trade a stock is the page's. A family runs on provisional settings, taken from published evidence and the operator's ruling, until its sweep proposes the values its freeze registers; its card says so until then, and nothing before the freeze counts toward a checkpoint (see: A family lists on provisional settings until its freeze, and nothing before the freeze counts toward a checkpoint). A freeze registers the family's live rule and its variants, each a whole rule evaluated every night at its own settings, keeping its own list and its own trades, and judged by the test its sweep's report fixed; and each family's correction for luck counts its own rules alone, so a rule added to one family moves no other family's level (see: A registered family rule is evaluated every night at its own settings and keeps its own list, its trades stored with their benchmark when they end) (see: Each setup family's correction for luck counts its own rules alone, at most nine a family).

Pullbacks are the swing filter of 11.2 as it stands: the names it passes, improving businesses first, each on the plan its trade gate read. Its freeze opens its base as the next filter version, the settings as they stood with a reward-to-risk floor raised, and registers the swing family again for that version (see: The pullback's freeze opens its base as the next filter version and registers the swing family again at one instant).

Breakouts. A member passes where the market check is open, its close is above the highest high of the half year of sessions before it, its volume is heavy against its fifty-session average, its daily ranges over the sessions before tonight were no wider than over the same count before them, and the night stores a typical move to place its stop by. It is bought at the close with its stop a stated count of typical moves beneath, and the stop trails the highest close since the buy at that distance and is never lowered; it has no target, and the trade ends at the first close under the stop or at the close of its last session. The names passing are ordered by their volume against its average, largest first. With no target a breakout sets itself no bar, so it has no win, no loss and no break-even: its result is what it made against what its plan put at risk, and its record is the average of that over its trades, its checkpoint test fixed in its sweep's report before its freeze (see: A breakout is a close above the year's high on heavy volume after its ranges narrowed, sold on a trailing stop with no target). Section 17 states each setting at the proposal its sweep made and its freeze registered, the half year's high, ranges narrowed to a share of the earlier ones and a nearer stop, and the provisional setting the freeze replaced, the year's high, ranges no wider and the wider stop, runs on as one of its variants (see: The new families freeze at their sweeps' proposals, the breakout's provisional setting and the drift's wider stop registered beside them as variants). Evidence: George and Hwang (2004) find nearness to the 52-week high predicts returns; Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin (2001) find a premium after unusually high volume; Dai, Marshall, Nguyen and Visaltanachoti (2021) find trailing stops cut downside risk for a lower average return, the wider ones surviving costs. Judgement: the volume multiple, the share of the earlier ranges the newer may reach, the half year's window and the stop's distance, none of which a study sets; each is the sweep's proposal over the history the store and the pulls hold, which the operator froze.

Earnings drift. A member passes where the market check is open, its newest print's reaction session is tonight or one of the few sessions before, the provider's surprise for that print is above zero, the reaction session closed up at least a stated share of the session before's typical move on heavy volume against its fifty-session average, and tonight's close is still above the reaction session's low. It is bought at the close and stopped at that low, and its target is the nearer of the lowest band far enough above the close and a stated multiple of the risk above it. The names passing are ordered by the surprise, largest first (see: The earnings drift buys a beat with a strong reaction within five sessions, stopped under the reaction session's low). It reads the reactions the move annotator stores from the calendar the night already fetches, so the night asks the provider for nothing more, and a print the calendar carries no actual for yet passes nothing until one is filed (see: Each print's reaction is read from the nightly calendar and the stored bars, and the earnings drift is the one rule that reads it). Section 17 states each setting at the proposal its sweep made and its freeze registered, a shorter window, a smaller reaction on heavier volume, and two of its variants are the provisional setting the freeze replaced and the proposal with its stop no closer than a typical move under the buy, moved down to that distance where the reaction's low sits nearer, since a stop at the low can sit a hair under the close (see: The new families freeze at their sweeps' proposals, the breakout's provisional setting and the drift's wider stop registered beside them as variants). Evidence: Bernard and Thomas (1989) find prices keep drifting toward a surprise for about sixty trading days, the largest surprises against the smallest; Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara and Venkatachalam (2008) find sorting on the announcement's own return earns more than sorting on the surprise, and both together more still. Both are about the largest surprises and a spread of long against short, not any beat bought alone. Judgement: the size of the reaction, the volume multiple, the window and the multiple of the risk, none of which a study sets.

Sector heavyweights are a rotation and not a swing setup: the largest companies of each sector that lead it, held while they lead. On each month's first session, or the first after it whose stored year holds the closes its readings need, each member is placed in the GICS sector the provider files, with the reclassification of 2023 read by date, and valued as the newest share count filed before the session times the session's close on the count's split basis; each sector's companies are ranked once a company, by the listing that traded the more dollars, and among a stated count of the largest the leaders are the stated count whose return over a stated look-back beats their sector's by the most, bought at that close where the lead is above nothing, the close sits above its 50-day average and that above its 200-day, and the stock's beta over 251 daily returns against the index is at least one; the sector's return is its fund's over the same look-back on the fund's own sessions (see: The sector heavyweights hold the largest companies leading their sectors, rotated on the first session of each month whose stored year holds the closes their readings need) (see: A heavyweight is bought where it leads its sector above nothing and passes the trend gate, and sold where the rule would not buy it) (see: The sector heavyweights freeze at their sweep's proposal, the proposal's three passing neighbours registered beside them as variants). A holding is sold at the close of a later month's rebalance where the rule would no longer buy it and at its last close as a member of the index, and a close under its 200-day average sells it only in the variant reading that exit (see: A heavyweight leaving the index is sold at its last session's close as a member). It has no stop and no target, so its result is its return in percent, carried night by night on adjusted closes, and its edge that return less the return of the size cut it was chosen from, each of the cut's companies weighted equally over the same sessions (see: A sector heavyweight's trade is scored by its percent return less the equal-weighted return of the size cut it was chosen from) (see: A heavyweight's result is the product of its daily close ratios since its buy, carried each night). The night values a member from the answer its quarters fetch already asks for and makes no request of its own, and reads the funds' and the index's closes its market series fetch stores, a rebalance waiting for the first night the store holds the night's close of each; and every rebalance waits for the first night the store's year holds the closes its readings need, a return or a beta over a number of sessions reading one close more than that number, which the year does not hold on a night whose date a year back was no session, and one reading no lead, or no beta where it reads one, waits the same way, so a short year sells nothing (see: The sector heavyweights hold the largest companies leading their sectors, rotated on the first session of each month whose stored year holds the closes their readings need) (see: The night values a member from its newest fetch, tonight's close brought to the count's basis by the fetch's own close) (see: The night asks for the market series' daily closes once a series, and keeps them apart from the members' bars). Its card is drawn after the swing families', reads no market check and keeps its own one holding a stock. The page's book holds at the setting the family's freeze registered, section 17 stating each, and each rule registered beside it, the live rule and its three variants, keeps a book of its own whose record the run page reads (see: Each registered sector heavyweights rule keeps a book of its own beside the page's, its holdings scored in percent against their size cut). Evidence: Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) find the industries with the highest six-month returns go on beating those with the lowest; Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) find stocks that beat over the past three to twelve months go on beating over the months after; Frazzini and Pedersen (2014) find stocks of high beta earned less for their risk, which the sweep's proposal reads against: over the pulled history its leaders did better with a beta of at least one than without it, a question its variants and its live record go on asking. Both momentum studies rank every stock and hold a tenth of them, not the largest few of a sector. Judgement: the ten largest, the twelve months' look-back, two leaders a sector, the fund, the beta's floor, a month between rebalances and the one exit are the sweep's proposal over the pulled history, which no study sets, and each of its neighbours that met the sweep's floors is registered beside it.

Sector leaders are a variant of the pullback and not a family of their own. The sectors are ranked each night by the median of their members' returns over the long span the swing readings store, a sector holding too few members with a return left unranked, and each member's own return is ranked inside its sector; the swing filter works the standings out and hands them to the pullback in the top three sectors, top quarter of each, the eighth rule of the swing family, which reads a member's standing in place of the trend and strength gate and is otherwise the pullback's whole rule, its trade the pullback's plan as the filter's row stored it (see: The sector leaders are a variant of the pullback's starting point and not a family of their own). Their sweep found that setting alone of its grid meeting the floors, every setting a step from it falling short, so it is a point and not a plateau, and it changes one thing in the pullback's rule; the membership names no sector for 319 of the 827 names the sweep read, so a name that left the index before its sector was filed stands in no ranking. Their card was drawn until the freeze, and a night that drew it is drawn as it was. Evidence: Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) find the industries with the highest six-month returns go on beating those with the lowest, and that industry momentum accounts for much of the momentum in single stocks. Judgement: the count of sectors against eleven where the study takes three of twenty industries, and the quarter.

The S&P 400 and 600, each with rules of its own. Every family runs on the S&P 400 and the S&P 600 as rules of their own, each index's strength ranked, market check read and edge measured among its own members, and the S&P 500's rules stay as frozen (see: The S&P 400 and 600 join the universe with rules of their own, since the first test showed only that the 500's settings do not carry to them). Their rules start on provisional settings with a price and a dollar volume floor and a profit gate (see: The 400 and 600 rules start provisional with liquidity floors and a profit gate before any testing), and every trade on them pays the effective spread published for its company's size and price (see: A 400 or 600 trade pays the published effective spread for its size and price, and its pass tests read the edge after it), taken off the trade and not its benchmark (see: A trade's cost comes off the trade and not its benchmark). Every member of the three indices carries each night every reading their rules and sweeps read, stored as it stood on the session with the market switches beside them, and the S&P 500's rules state each record's edge after each trade's own round trip beside it, their records unchanged. Evidence: why each index needs settings of its own. Prices now take in an earnings surprise on the day it is announced, the drift after it gone from large companies since 2006 and more recently from smaller ones (Martineau (2022)), and where it lasted it sat in the least liquid stocks, whose costs took 70 to 100 per cent of its paper profits (Chordia, Goyal, Sadka, Sadka and Shivakumar (2009)), which is why the drift's card on the 400 and 600 states the evidence against it (see: The 400's and 600's earnings drift lists from the first night with the evidence against it on its card). Momentum's profits fall sharply with size past the very smallest companies and run longer where fewer analysts follow a stock, mostly among past losers (Hong, Lim and Stein (2000)). Nearness to the 52-week high predicts returns (George and Hwang (2004)), the effect held in small stocks (Barroso and Wang (2021)) and a recent high adding to it (Bhootra and Hur (2013)). The size premium holds steady once low-quality companies are controlled for (Asness, Frazzini, Israel, Moskowitz and Pedersen (2018)). Short-term reversals are stronger among smaller stocks (Dai, Medhat, Novy-Marx and Rizova (2024)). Big firms lead small ones within an industry, mainly in taking in bad news (Hou (2007)), and investors overreact to early reporters' news for late reporters until the late reporters' own report (Thomas and Zhang (2008)), so a swing rule may keep off a small company whose industry's large ones have just fallen (see: A 400 or 600 swing pick may be kept off where its industry's S&P 500 heavyweights fell, a dial its sweeps test). Most factors are positively autocorrelated, the average earning more after a positive year (Ehsani and Linnainmaa (2022)), and small stocks carry more of the default spread's risk than large ones (Fama and French (1989)). A company of $1 to 5 billion pays an effective spread of about 0.06 to 0.24 per cent by its price (Collver (2014)), an S&P 500 company about 0.03 (Hagströmer), and the estimators read from daily highs and lows overstate both, which is why the published table is read and not an estimate (Ardia, Guidotti and Kroencke (2024)). S&P admits a company to the 400 or 600 only on positive earnings over its last four quarters and its latest (S&P Dow Jones Indices (2020)), so the profit gate leaves out few of today's members. Judgement: that a breakout fails more often among smaller stocks, which no study states; the size factor's own momentum, and the credit switch's 50 sessions and three months, none shown on its own; and the price floor, the dollar volumes and the cost's doubling. Each is a dial or a switch a sweep reads after costs, and none is frozen before the operator's go.

12. The research runner and its staleness rules

Figure 12.1. What happens when you open a name. Most of the time, nothing is spent.
Computed sections appearchart, levels, plan, numbers, dates, straight from tonight's store with no waiting
→
Is there a research record?no: offer to write one, and show the report complete without the narrative sections. yes: continue
→
Does it still stand?four questions, all answered from data already stored: has a new filing appeared, has the earnings date passed, has the news pulse for this name jumped above its own baseline, did you press refresh
→
All four noshow the stored research with its as-of date, spend nothing, done
A pass is warrantedread this name's filings since the last record, its news since then, and its theme record, refreshing the theme first if that is what went stale
→
Write the sectionsthe short version, what the company sells, the industry cycle, the two cases, the risks, the cause column of the moves table, and the dated calendar items
→
Check every claima number must be in the facts file; a claim must name a source document that is in the store; a section failing twice is left out rather than guessed
→
Store itnew record with today's as-of date, the previous record kept, every source document kept

Key. The four staleness questions are all free, because the nightly run already computed their inputs. That is the point of putting the news pulse counter in the nightly half of figure 5.1: deciding not to spend money must not cost money. (see: Deciding not to spend must not cost anything)

Nothing expires on a timer. A timer either refreshes work nobody needed or serves research written before a print. A filing, an earnings date, a jump in coverage or your own judgement are the only things that can make analysis out of date, and all four are observable.

The previous record is kept rather than overwritten, so the app can show that the two cases were rewritten after a print and what they said before. It also means a report you showed someone last month can be reproduced. (see: Research is a stored document with an as-of date, not a cache)

The claim checker is what makes model-written analysis usable. Numbers are checked against the facts file, which is the same rule the computed sections live by. Claims are checked differently, by requiring that the document supporting them was stored, which is why the source list in section 4 is a design requirement rather than a courtesy. An unsupported claim is dropped, because the failure mode of automated research is a confident wrong sentence and nothing else in the system would catch it. (see: Every researched claim must name a stored source document)

Every section is asked the same way. Its ask is said again after the documents and the sections already written, under "Now write the section:", with a retry's brief after it. The instructions name the reader as someone deciding whether to hold a swing trade in the stock over the next weeks to few months, so a section keeps what could move the stock before and at its next report, and they say that what a figure only a document gives shows is said without the number. An answer holding nothing but citation markers is no answer. Each document listed carries its kind beside its title, a company filing or release, a news report, or an opinion or promotional piece, read from its address, and an opinion piece is cited only for what its writer argues. The two cases and the risks are each given a weak point and a strong one with no digit in them. A review, which ships naming DeepSeek over three reports, asks the model that wrote the two cases or the risks to check its own draft against the section's rules and revise it, beside the report and never in it. The drafts a trial or a review writes, each section's rates over the ten reports each side of the addendum's merge and the two cases' figures on both sides over the twenty reports since their ask changed are written to files by a command, and no page draws them. (see: The research prompt repeats each section's ask after the documents, names its reader and marks each document by kind) (see: A review asks a section's model to check its own draft against the section's rules, beside a stated number of reports) (see: The drafts compared beside a report and the research template's before and after counts are written to files by a command, and drawn on no page)

12.2 How one pass splits between the two models

Key. The green boxes on the left run on the operator's own machine and cost nothing. The purple boxes on the right are the only part of the whole system that spends money. The red box is the check every section must pass before it can be stored, and the blue-topped box at the bottom is the record itself.

Where the line falls is decided by one test: is the answer inside a single document, or does it have to be built across several that disagree. The business explainer and the segment commentary are extraction from a filing already fetched, and the key under each figure explains values already computed. Those are small jobs a local model does reliably, and each call carries a few thousand tokens rather than the whole evidence set, which is what makes a consumer graphics card sufficient for that lane at all. Naming what caused a large move reads the few documents code picked out inside it, which the test puts on the left, and the fixture comparison moved it right on this machine: over one evidence set the local model wrote figures from the articles that the facts file does not hold, again after being told why, where the paid model's first draft was accepted (see: The fixture comparison moved the cause of each large move into the paid lane on this machine). The right-hand lane needs every document in memory at once, which is why the paid model does it. (see: A research pass is split by section difficulty, not run wholesale on one model)

The consequence for cost is that a pass buys a fraction of the paid work rather than all of it. This said that the figures in section 17 are an upper bound rather than an estimate, and section 17 carries no per-pass cost figure to be a bound on: what it carries is the cap, which is a stop rather than an estimate of what a pass costs. So the consequence is stated against the cap instead. A pass buying a fraction of the paid work means the cap binds later than it would if the whole pass were paid, and what a pass actually costs is a measurement the spend ledger takes rather than a figure written here (owes: The spend cap set from the passes the ledger has priced).

Which sections sit in which lane is a setting rather than a structure. On the machine this is first built for, the left lane holds classification and extraction and the right lane holds everything else. On a machine able to hold a large model with a long context, sections move left and a pass writes them for nothing. The picture is the same either way; only the boundary moves. (see: The local lane's scope is a setting, and whatever it holds is written for nothing) (see: The local and paid boundary is a property of the machine, not of the design)

What each lane actually writes

Every section is made in the same three steps. Code works out the figures and picks the documents the section may rest on. A model writes the words around them, and is never asked for a number or a date. The claim checker then refuses the section unless every figure in it is one code computed and every sentence rests on a document it is allowed to rest on (see: Code owns every number), and it refuses a sentence carrying the word the corpus bans, in any form, or an em dash, as it refuses one resting on nothing (see: A written sentence carrying the word the corpus bans or an em dash is refused as an uncited one is). Every model is told to describe the company and never to prescribe: no section proposes a trade, a holding, adding, trimming or a plan for income, because the plan is computed by code and drawn in its own region (see: A written section describes the company and never proposes a trade, a holding or a plan for income). The table says what each step does for each section. The lane is this machine's default and is a setting; the rest of a row stays the same when a section moves lane.

SectionLaneWhat code works out firstWhat the model is asked to writeWhat it must pass to be stored
The cause of each large movepaidthe largest moves of the stored year from the bars, each with its percentage change, the session it ended on and the session its change was measured from; moves whose spans share a session read as one episode; then, for each episode, the documents fetched for the name that were published inside its largest move, at most two a move, a title naming the company first, then the newest, then the fewest companies named, and none older than three months before the night (see: A research pass reads a name's news from the last three months alone, inside each stored move and since the company's own filing, and hands each section the documents code picks from it). The risks, each with what would confirm itpaidthe same whole seteach risk the documents support returned as fields, the risk with the document stating it, what would be seen if it came true, being a listed fact's name with the direction it moves and the level it crosses wherever a fact could show it and an event with one kind of seven where none could, and why with the document saying so, which code composes into a paragraph a risk opening on its ordinal and a sentence opening "That risk would be confirmed by"; a valuation risk confirmed by the multiple falling and never by it staying high, and never a level the next quarter crosses by construction (see: Each risk is returned as fields and confirmed by a listed fact or an event of one kind, and no two risks share either)the same two rules, the level held to the facts file as a figure is; an answer not returned as its fields, a fact the file does not list, a kind outside the seven, and two risks confirmed by one fact or two by events of one kind, are refused

Why each section sits in its lane. The three local sections each have their answer in one place: one filing, the segment table, or values already computed. Each call carries only those, a few thousand tokens, which is what makes a consumer graphics card enough for that lane. The cause of each large move has its answer in the few documents inside one move as well, and sits in the paid lane on this machine because the comparison measured the local model failing it there. The five other paid sections are built across documents that disagree. Which risks are live, what the two cases are and what they come to cannot be read out of one document, and a small model given contradictory evidence produces something fluent that says nothing. A dated item is a claim resting on a source rather than a provider event, and deciding which of several documents dates a thing is a judgement across them (see: A calendar event is fetched once for the whole index, and the calendar holds provider events only). The industry cycle is paid for a reason of its own: it is written from a record every name in its industry shares, and that record is built by a paid pass of its own (see: Industry research is per theme, not per name). After the split the two lanes are the same: both pass one claim checker and land in one research record, each section carrying its own date and the model that wrote it.
