What a retry is told, and what stands where a section is left out. A section the checker refuses is asked for again in the same pass, up to three times, each retry told each thing the draft before it was refused for on a line of its own, the figure, date, citation or sentence with the sentence it sits in, the rule, and what to do: a figure or a date removed or replaced by one the facts file lists, a number written in words also said with no number and no count word, a sentence citing nothing removed or ended on the marker of the document that states it. The refused draft is read again by the checker's rules over the facts file and the source list it was checked against, so the lines are the findings the checker stored, and the draft itself is never pasted back, because a retry told only the reason wrote new figures in place of the one it was refused for. A refusal at the third retry leaves the section out, and its reason says the last retry repeated what it was told where it did (see: A retry names each thing the check refused, and a section refused on its third retry is left out). On the day a report was written, a regenerate writes the sections that report left out and none it accepted (see: A regenerate on the day a report was written writes only the sections that report left out, and a report the connection cut is not the day's). The short version is written last, from the sections the checker accepted, held to the facts file as every section is; the section a reader reads first is never empty, since where no accepted one stands the page draws a summary code writes from computed parts alone and says why it stands there (see: The short version is written last from the sections that passed, and one left out is replaced by a summary code writes). The two cases are asked for reasons rather than restated figures, for each change with its size, and for each fact on one side only, and a draft arguing one figure on both sides is not refused, since one figure can rightly stand on both; a draft whose case for and case against cannot be told apart is refused (see: The two cases are asked to argue a fact on one side only, and a draft doing otherwise is counted rather than refused).

13. How the picks improve

Measuring something is not the same as improving it, and until this section the document only measured. This is the loop. It is deliberately small: one score per condition, one register of candidates, and one column in a table that already exists. No new component runs nightly, no new store is needed beyond what the listings already hold, and none of it is built before the evidence exists to run it.

13.1 The score, and why it is not a return

Every listing already carries a plan, and a plan states an entry, a stop and a target. That makes each listing a falsifiable prediction with a bar it must clear, computed from its own arithmetic and nothing else.

Take the worked example's first tranche. Entry near 920, stop on a close below 855, first traded target at 1057. Risk is 65 points, reward is 137, so the setup breaks even if the target is reached before the stop about 32% of the time. That number is not a preference or a benchmark borrowed from elsewhere; it falls out of where the bands sit.

The 920 in that arithmetic is the midpoint of the entry zone. It is where the plan's own figures are computed and it is not where any record is scored. A setup is scored from the close of the session it was listed on, admitted only where that close sits inside the plan's own range, and the break-even stored beside its outcome is measured from that close rather than from the midpoint (see: A stored break-even is measured from the close the setup was entered at, as a percentage beside the figures it is compared with) (see: An entry is admitted only inside the plan's own range, and a plan with no entry zone takes its whole range as its zone). So a plan states one break-even and each of its setups stores another, and the two are different numbers about different entries: the first is what the plan demanded on the evening it was drawn, and the second is the bar that setup is judged against. Section 10 says what the midpoint is for and what it is never used for.

So the question asked of every condition is: across all the setups it produced, did the target come before the stop more often than the mean of the break-evens stored with them required. That is one number, it is a count of stored rows, and it is meaningful in a way a forward return is not. Twenty-one-day returns mostly measure whether the market went up, which is why the run page shows them against the universe base rate. This score has no such problem, because the bar moves with the setup. (see: A condition is judged against the break-even its own plan demands)

Key. Green boxes are computed nightly from stored bars, and the grey boxes at the right of the row are the cases that matter most: a setup whose price never came back to its entry and a setup that has done nothing yet are neither wins nor losses. Counting either as one would flatter or punish a condition for a trade that did not happen. A setup starts on the first close at or below its entry zone's top edge and is held open until the target hits, the stop hits, or the time cap expires. A target reached before that close is never entered, and a timed-out setup is reported separately, and neither is ever a win (see: A setup is scored from its entry, and a target reached before the entry is never a win).

The bar in the second box is computed from the plan itself. A setup with a distant target and a tight stop needs to be right rarely; one with a near target and a wide stop needs to be right often. Comparing conditions on wins alone would reward the second kind for nothing, which is why the score is always relative to what each setup demanded. (see: The significance threshold is divided by the family size, and the divisor is shown)

13.2 Three things that can improve, shallowest first

What changesHow it is decidedPhase
Condition thresholdsthe swing filter's thresholds, each moved only by a shape calibration the operator accepts, to the value that puts its gate's median count over the ordinary nights inside its band (see: The swing filter's shape is calibrated over its ordinary nights, a night one cause pushes past a quarter and twice its usual share is left out, and each band spans a third to three times what the ruled filter passes). Changes how long the list is more than how good it isnone. It waits on 60 ordinary nights under one filter version, read on the run page's Calibration region, which 12.3 builds (owes: The swing filter's shape calibrated from its ordinary nights)
Which conditions exista condition whose setups fail to clear their own break-even over enough resolved cases is retired; a new one is registered and scored in shadow until it has earned promotion (see: A live reason is added or retired only by a change to section 11 and the code together, and the register holds candidates alone)8, at the register and the shadow column
The ladder rulesthe merge distance, where the stop sits, the near-exit skip, and whether a zone's edges come from its non-average anchors alone. Each is a named rule version, and because the bars are stored every night can be scored under every version at once8, at rule versions scored counterfactually

Only the first is cheap enough to do without resolved setups, and it is the one that matters least: it needs sixty ordinary nights of the swing filter's gate counts, where the other two need setups that have reached a target or a stop. All three wait on the calendar rather than on a checkpoint, which is why the other two sit in phase 8 and why phase 5 has an obligation described below. A fourth row stood here until 8.0, the model's own proposal stored beside the computed plan and scored with it, and it is dropped rather than carved out of the rule that no model is asked for a number (see: The model writes no entry or exit proposal, and the loop scores only what code computes).

13.3 The guardrails

The danger in a loop like this is not that it fails to find anything. It is that it finds something that is not there. Run five candidate conditions of no real value and the chance that at least one clears an ordinary significance test is about 23%; run twenty and it is 64%. Picking the best of twenty noise processes and shipping it is the standard way a self-improving system makes itself worse while appearing to learn.

So the rules below are written before any data exists, which is the only time they can be written without knowing which way the answer would go.

GuardrailRuleWhat it prevents
Registered in advanceevery candidate condition is written to the append-only register with its rule, its test and the date, before it is scored. The family has a stated maximum sizechoosing what to test after seeing which way the data went
Corrected for the familythe significance threshold is divided by the number of registered candidates, and the divisor is recorded with the verdictone of many candidates clearing a test by chance and being read as a finding
Minimum resolved setupsno verdict of any kind below the stated minimum; a higher minimum before a live condition may be retired (see: A live reason is added or retired only by a change to section 11 and the code together, and the register holds candidates alone)acting on a handful of cases, where almost any result is possible
Unresolved is never a wina setup that has neither hit its target nor its stop within the time cap is reported in its own column and excluded from the ratethe same failure as counting an unexamined harness claim as a pass
Shadow before liveno condition appears on the list until its record has crossed the boundary of a look, and no candidate's pick of a name is shown anywhere but the Run page's comparison of tonight's picks (see: Candidate conditions are registered before they are scored, and a candidate's picks are shown on the Run page while its outcomes wait for a look). A candidate's own record is drawn on the run page, beside the candidate and never beside a name, with the nightly figure labelled as monitoring and the verdict field changed only by a look (see: The nightly running figure is monitoring and never the verdict)adopting an idea on the strength of the idea, and reading a running figure as a verdict
Frozen windowsa rule or threshold is not changed during a window it is being measured over. A change starts a new window and the old one is kept (see: A reason's record reads only the rows written under the threshold the code carries, and the rows written under another are kept)a measurement whose subject moved while it was being measured
Adding restarts the clockregistering a new candidate after the family is set inflates the family, so the correction changes and the affected verdicts are recomputedquietly widening the search until something passes
Every change is recordeda promotion, a retirement or a rule version change is written with the evidence that produced it and the version it replaced (see: A live reason is added or retired only by a change to section 11 and the code together, and the register holds candidates alone)a system that drifts without anyone able to say why

Key. Read it downward. The blue-topped box at the top is the register, an append-only table that accepts new dated rows and never edits or deletes one. The green box below it is the only nightly work, and it is the same arithmetic the live conditions already do, just written to a shadow column instead of the list. The two orange boxes are gates rather than steps: a candidate stalls at them rather than failing, and stalling forever is a perfectly good outcome.

The left-hand exits are where most candidates end up, and that is the point. A grey exit means not enough has happened yet and nothing is claimed either way. A red exit means the evidence arrived and the idea did not survive it, so the candidate is retired with its record kept, which is what stops the same idea being proposed again in a year.

13.4 What each phase owes

The loop is a phase 8 feature. But it cannot be added in phase 8 unless phase 5 stores the right things, because the evidence takes months to accumulate and cannot be recreated afterwards.

Phase 5 must record, for every listing, the plan as it stood that night: the entry zone, the stop and the first traded target. Storing only which reasons fired is not enough. Without the plan there is no break-even, and without the break-even none of the scoring in this section is possible. The bars can be replayed but the plan cannot, because by the time phase 8 arrives the rules may have changed and recomputing would score old listings under new rules. This is one JSON column written by a component that is already running, and it is the difference between phase 8 being a feature and phase 8 being a six-month wait.

Beyond that the phases carry what their table already says. Phase 5 records how many names fire each night, which is what the thresholds are calibrated against later; the calibration is not phase 5's work, because it waits on sixty nights of that record and no checkpoint accumulates nights. Phase 8 adds the scoring, the register, the shadow column, the rule versions scored counterfactually and the run page's condition verdicts, which is one new nightly component, the rule version scorer, and three new stores, the candidate register, the rule versions and the version scores. Nothing a reader sees changes but the run page.

13.5 The boundary this must not cross

Section 1 says the list selects the stocks worth buying or paying attention to that evening, so a change that makes the selection better is inside this project, including one that orders names against each other. (see: Tonight's list selects the stocks worth buying or paying attention to that evening, and the improvement loop exists to make that selection better) The boundary is what a change may use and where its result may be shown. The nightly run stays arithmetic, with no model call and no per-name request. (see: The nightly run is arithmetic only) No reading of the fundamentals fires a reason or gates a tranche, and the one that orders anything is the state a company's reported quarters give it, which orders tonight's list and removes no name from it. (see: Four readings of a member's reported quarters are worked out every night by rules the measured split settled, and its state is read from sales and operating margin alone) The plan places a position and never sizes one. (see: The plan places a position and never sizes one) A rule's record is shown under the rule's own heading and never as the stock's own, beside its reason or on a pick's card. (see: A rule's record is drawn under the rule's own heading, beside its reason or on a pick's card and never as the stock's own) A condition is registered before it is scored and scored in shadow before its results are shown, its picks alone drawn on the Run page before a look, and the register is never edited. (see: Candidate conditions are registered before they are scored, and a candidate's picks are shown on the Run page while its outcomes wait for a look)

13.6 How a candidate is judged

Each setup carries its own bar, as section 13.1 says, and the bar is its null win probability: the chance a plan with no edge reaches its target before its stop, simulated from the plan under the name's trailing volatility with the 63-session cap and a round trip of 10 basis points, with the planned break-even shown beside it (see: A setup's null win probability is calibrated from its own plan, and its planned break-even is shown beside it). Both barriers are judged on closes, so a close lands past either and the realized exit is not the planned one. Evidence: Broadie, Glasserman and Kou (1997) and Janssen and van Leeuwaarden (2007) give the limiting expected overshoot of a zero-drift Gaussian walk checked at discrete times as about 0.5826 of one step's standard deviation, a benchmark and not a measurement of these names; Lopez de Prado (2018) frames an outcome by a profit barrier, a stop and a time barrier, which the yardstick matches, and realized loss in multiples of planned risk is reported beside every verdict and tested nowhere. Judgement: a simulation in which a no-edge plan wins about 38.3% at a stop one typical move away against a planned 35%, and about 30.5% at three moves, so a worthless condition with tight stops could clear the planned break-even.

The 10 basis points is pinned into the calibration and 30 is shown as a sensitivity; close-based scoring assumes a fill at the exact close, which no order type guarantees, and stop-outs on earnings sessions are reported apart (see: The calibrated null carries a round trip of ten basis points, and thirty is shown as a sensitivity). Evidence: Hagstromer on the S&P 500's effective spread, about 3.2 basis points; Schwarz et al. on retail round trips from about 7; Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz on institutional large-cap costs of about 18 to 30 round trip; Arratia and Dorador (2019) that overnight gaps above 0.1% occur on about 78% of days with a mean near zero, so the direction of the close-fill bias is unknown; Dubinsky et al. (2019) that earnings-day variance ran about six times other days over 2000 to 2015. Judgement: the choice of 10 among those figures. Not settled by research: what the closing auction costs an S&P 500 name (closing-auction costs).

A setup entered and stopped in one session is a loss with no figure and no break-even, and a candidate's record counts it as a loss, its null taken from the zone's high edge, the worst fill in the zone, with the count shown beside the verdict; the store held 8 of 254 losses in that shape (see: A candidate counts a setup entered and stopped in one session as a loss). Judgement: the high edge, since the store does not say where in the zone the fill was. Not settled by research: whether the live family should count them too, which is the operator's to rule (the live family's same-session losses).

Setups are not independent: listings cluster by date, and setups listed less than 63 sessions apart resolve over shared bars. So the unit is a block of 63 consecutive calendar sessions keyed on the listing date, and the verdict is a sign-flip test over the blocks: each block's summed excess of wins over null probabilities, T the mean over its standard error, and the p-value the share of all 2^q sign vectors, the identity included, at least as large, every one of them enumerated since q is at most 16 (see: A candidate is judged by a sign-flip test over blocks of 63 sessions, with at least eight blocks). A permutation of outcomes across setups is not the test, because it always returns 1. The Poisson-binomial p-value is shown beside it, labelled, and decides nothing. Evidence: Kolari and Pynnonen (2010) on event-date clustering making standard tests over-reject; Lopez de Prado (2018) on overlapping outcome windows; Canay, Romano and Shaikh (2017) that sign changes are the transformation group for a location null, valid with a fixed number of large clusters; MacKinnon, Nielsen and Webb (2023) on its close relation to the restricted wild cluster bootstrap, whose sign-flip scheme it shares; Cameron, Gelbach and Miller (2008) that the wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed holds size where cluster-robust Wald tests over-reject, in simulations of up to 30 clusters. Not settled by research: an always-valid test under this clustering (an always-valid test), and whether the live family's own test should change (the live family's test).

At least 8 non-empty blocks are needed, only non-empty blocks count, the length is registered with the candidate and never shortened by the data, and the block count is shown against its minimum wherever the resolved count is; 8 blocks is 504 sessions, about two years, plus up to 63 for the last to resolve. Evidence: Ibragimov and Mueller (2010) that groups are consecutive observations and the choice of group cannot be delegated to the data; Cameron and Miller (2015) that p-values are discrete with few clusters, and the design effect, actual variance over the variance under simple random sampling, which they give from Kish; no moving-block or stationary bootstrap is the verdict (Kuensch (1989)). Judgement: the floor of 8 blocks, where a one-sided sign-flip floor of 1/2^q needs 6 to reach a third of 0.05 at all. Not settled by research: whether dependence runs longer than 63 sessions through a market regime (dependence through a regime), and whether the block should be a multiple of the outcome window (the block length multiple).

A verdict is read only at looks fixed at registration, at 8, 12 and 16 blocks, information fractions of 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0, triggered by the block count and never by the figure, with the level spent across them by an O'Brien-Fleming-type function and each look's boundary found on the sign-flip null by enumerating every arrangement of the signs of the blocks it holds, which at sixteen blocks is exact and assumes nothing about what the setups inside a block did to each other (see: A candidate's verdict is read only at looks fixed when it is registered, with each look's boundary found over every sign vector its blocks allow). The first look cannot promote: the level released at 0.5 is 0.00071, below the 1/256 that 8 blocks allow, so it can only retire. The earliest promotion is at 12 blocks, 756 sessions, and the last look at 16, 1,008 sessions, each plus up to 63. Evidence: Armitage, McPherson and Rowe (1969) on repeated tests on accumulating data; Lan and DeMets (1983) on spending functions chosen before monitoring; O'Brien and Fleming (1979); FDA (2019) that analysis times chosen from results inflate error and that a maximum is not extended. Judgement: the three looks and their spacing; under independence at a 35% break-even, reading every three resolved setups instead would reach a size of 7.4% by 1,000.

A look counts only setups whose whole outcome window has closed, its cut-off at least the entry window plus 63 sessions back and stored with the verdict (see: A look counts only the setups whose whole outcome window has closed). Evidence: by analogy, Hampson and Jennison (2013) on pipeline subjects at interim analyses and Lindon and Kallus (2026) on outcome-dependent censoring. Judgement: a simulation in which wins take 22.9 sessions to resolve and losses 16.0, so an early record undercounts wins, which the store's 109 wins in 355 scored setups against a median break-even of 39.1% shows.

A candidate is retired by a nonbinding futility guideline at its first or second look, where its win share is strictly below its null share, or by reaching its last look without crossing, each by a new dated row; the promotion boundary ignores the guideline (see: A candidate is retired by a futility guideline at its first two looks or by reaching its last look). Evidence: FDA (2019) on nonbinding futility and Lan and DeMets (1983) on conditional power. Judgement: the strictness, which under independence retires 61.8% of worthless candidates by the second look and a candidate with a true 4.6-point excess 7.3% of the time.

The level at Holm's first step is 0.05 over the distinct trials, shared across every one of them for the life of the system and never given fresh to a window, the trials of each setup family counted apart from every other family's (see: Each setup family's correction for luck counts its own rules alone, at most nine a family): a distinct trial is a rule whose results a look has read or that is still running, a registration of the same rule where only the version it reads changed is the trial it replaces, and a candidate retired with no result of its own read is counted in none, as the three registered on 2026-09-23 were not once the swing family's nine (section 13.8) registered (see: The three phase 10 candidates are retired when the swing family registers, and each retirement says no result of theirs was read); each candidate spends its level across its own looks, a look is read at the count as of the night it was read, and a trial registered since moves only the looks not yet read; each candidate is read in the window it opened with and in no later one holding it beside a candidate registered since, and a candidate no night has evaluated has opened no window and is read over the candidates standing beside it, the ones the next night evaluates with it, or, where it was retired first, the ones standing when it was retired; a graph in each register row passes a promoted candidate's level in equal shares to those standing and a retired one's to no one, the promoted stepping first in the order their promotions were written and candidates crossing on one read after them in the order they were registered (see: The graph steps promoted candidates in the order their promotions were written, and candidates crossing on one read in the order they were registered), only the sign-flip p-value is corrected, and beside each verdict stand the step, its level and the count of distinct trials, the count and the level it sets standing beside the family's divisor too (see: Holm's level passes between the candidates by a graph fixed when they are registered, and its first step is 0.05 over the distinct trials read at a look or still running). Evidence: Holm (1979) and Romano and Wolf (2005) on step-down control; Maurer and Bretz (2013) on passing a level by a pre-specified graph under group-sequential designs, with sequential p-values as Liu and Anderson (2008) give them, as cited there; Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016), Bailey and Lopez de Prado (2014), Tian and Ramdas and Sullivan, Timmermann and White (1999) on counting every trial. Judgement: the budget shared across the trials, which the operator ruled: at every look the levels the counted trials hold sum to 0.05, and a trial a look has read is counted for the life of the system, so no window starts with a fresh 0.05 where the per-window level let lifetime error grow with every window; a verdict keeps the bar it was read at, so trials registered after others were read are read at the larger count while the earlier keep theirs, six read at 0.05 over 6 and six registered after them at 0.05 over 12 coming to at most 0.075.

The nightly running figure is shown on the run page labelled as monitoring, and the verdict field shows the last look's result, the looks remaining and what triggers the next (see: The nightly running figure is monitoring and never the verdict). Evidence: FDA (2019) recommends limiting access to interim results. Judgement: the operator chose to show it knowingly, and a figure labelled monitoring beside a field that only a look changes keeps the two apart.

Nothing a candidate or version is registered with changes while it runs: the calibration's paths and seed, the cost, the spending function, the looks, the graph and the method each look's boundary is found by are fixed before the registration command runs, and settling a proposed number is a new registration (see: Nothing a candidate or a version is registered with changes while it runs, and a proposed number is settled only by a new registration). Evidence: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016): a choice made after the running figure has been seen is a free parameter. Judgement: the store's realized loss and gain by stop distance is measured over live listings before registration, never over a candidate's outcomes.

13.7 What the judging can and cannot show

A single read at 250 independent setups, at a 35% break-even and one-sided 0.05 over three, needs a 9.45-point excess for 80% power and has 23.8% power against 4.6 points, the edge published levels showed over arbitrary ones, and 10.2% against 2.9, the edge left five days on if the arbitrary baseline held; at design effects of 1.25 to 3 the 80% figure rises to 10.72 to 16.00 points (see: Power is stated for the looks that exist as well as for a single read). Evidence: Osler (2000): published levels bounced 60.8% of the time against 56.2% for arbitrary ones, and five days after publication 1.7 points less often than on the day. Judgement: the looks that exist hold far more setups than 250: simulated with the level split conservatively between the second and third looks and the edge steady across blocks, arrived and narrow at about 161 setups a block detects a 4.6-point excess 98% of the time at design effect 1 and 65% at 3, and the others 92% to 100%; the first look has no power by construction, heterogeneity across blocks would lower every figure, and each is re-derived on the calibrated null before registration and re-read at every look.

13.8 The swing filter's two clocks

The list's thresholds move only through shape calibration and the operator's rulings, and the edge clock gathers evidence and changes nothing until it can retire a variant, after about two years, or promote one, after about three. The shape clock tunes how many names each gate passes and may recompute what the list would have been from the stored gate readings, because it moves counts and reads no outcome; it waits on sixty ordinary nights under one filter version, event nights set aside (see: The swing filter's shape is calibrated over its ordinary nights, a night one cause pushes past a quarter and twice its usual share is left out, and each band spans a third to three times what the ruled filter passes). The edge clock judges whether the filter's setups reach their target before their stop more often than their own bar, by the blocks and looks section 13.6 states, and never recomputes anything. At the shape clock's trigger the shape proposer proposes one setting a gate and applies none of them; the operator accepts or rejects the proposal with the shape command, and an acceptance opens the next filter version and, once the live filter's candidate stands registered, restarts its edge clock, bounded as section 17 states (see: The shape proposer moves one setting a gate, nearest first, and never applies what it proposes) (see: A shape acceptance restarts the live filter's edge clock, and after one acceptance while the list is live each further one states the blocks it restarts).

From 12.5 the family is the swing filter's: the live filter at the open filter version's settings and its variants, each the same whole rule with one thing moved and named for the version it was defined against, the sixth leaving off a member whose reported quarters read deteriorating, a state no gate reads, from 13.9 the seventh reading a member's standing in its sector in place of the trend and strength gate, and from the operator's ruling of 2026-10-02 the eighth keeping, of the members it fires on a night, the first three in the list's own order, nine candidates judged by the same sign-flip test over blocks and looks, each starting at 0.05 over the distinct trials section 13.6 counts, each evaluated in the filter's own stage over every member's gate inputs and stored on the member's row (see: The swing filter's trade gate reads section 10's plan for the swing trade, and the plan at the nearest bands is the variant in the reward to risk variant's place) (see: A variant of the swing filter is registered as a whole rule and runs on unchanged when the live settings move) (see: The sector leaders are a variant of the pullback's starting point and not a family of their own). Each rule's record keeps one open trade a stock of its own, free the night after the trade ends (see: A stock holds one open trade on each rule's list, and it is free the night after its trade ends), and the best three's record keeps the first three a night once its own open trades have kept a stock off, a member past them no trade; the family takes a new rule by being registered again whole at one instant under the version already open (see: The pullback's ninth rule keeps the night's best three in the list's own order, and the family is registered again whole to add it). Phase 10's three are retired by the command that registers the family, at the same instant, each retirement stating that no result of the candidate it retires was read before it (see: The three phase 10 candidates are retired when the swing family registers, and each retirement says no result of theirs was read).

From 12.7 the edge half of the run page's Calibration region states each swing family candidate's non-empty blocks against the 8 its first look is read at, its resolved setups and, from that floor on, its share of setups reaching target before stop against its planned break-even and its calibrated null, the variants each with the filter version they were defined against and the settings the live filter has moved since (owes: The swing family's first look). A candidate's setups are the swing filter rows it fired on, each scored on the plan its trade gate read (see: A swing filter row carries both swing plans, each scored from the night's close, and a candidate's setups are scored on the plan its own trade gate reads). Beside it, the near misses set each gate's and each exclusion's rejected setups against the setups the filter admitted (see: A gate's near misses are the setups it alone rejected, each group read against its own break-even and null and withheld below the block floor). Both read what the nights stored, and neither reaches the recount the shape clock may make, so the edge clock changes nothing and nothing it reads is moved by a setting changed since.

13.9 The sweep that proposes a starting point

The swing filter's live rule was set by hand, and the operator's ruling of 2026-09-29 asks for it to be set instead from a starting point the stored history supports, without fitting it to that history: the sweep replays the filter over every session the store and the pulled history hold, across every design the structural choices make and every setting of the nine dials, and proposes a starting point and the variants that run beside it (see: A starting point is proposed from the deepest setting of a plateau on the edge and never its best variation, and nothing is registered before the operator approves it). A design is one choice of each structural axis: the strength measure, the live classifier at each of its four versions or one of three simpler uptrend rules, the kind of support, the pullback's reference high, the trigger, the stop and target rule, the exit and the earnings window. Section 17's sweep rows state the grid, the edge, the conditions, the point-in-time check, the search, the floors a starting point is held to, the four tests a variant passes and how the run looks after itself. Every reading the live design takes is the live rule's own function; the other choices are the same function over another window, band or trigger, and Wilder's averages are seeded where the night's year of bars begins on each session, as the night seeds them.

Every result is read as an edge: the trade's result less what the same plan, entered at the same session's close on every member the index held that night, came to under the same exit, since a walk with no drift averages minus the round trip whatever the market did (see: The sweep ranks on the edge over the same plan entered on every member, with one open trade a stock and seven conditions tested in steps). One open trade a stock holds inside every variation, as the pages' rule holds it, so every setting is one walk over its design's candidates in name and session order rather than a cell of a cumulative table, which cannot apply the rule. Before the first stage a sample of the name-sessions is rebuilt with the night's own components over scratch stores and compared exactly, and any difference stops the run. The first stage reads every design at three values of each dial and ranks the designs by the median edge of their viable settings; each of seven conditions read as the data stood on the session, near the 52-week high, the sector's strength, the turn-up day's volume, a momentum reset, a recent earnings beat, tightening and the pullback's shape, is then tried alone on the ten strongest designs and survives where enough of them keep it, every survivor is crossed on and off with the designs and their structural neighbours, and the five strongest rows go to the second stage with the survivors as dials. The second stage searches each design by sampling its grid, fixes the plateau's line under the best edge, measures depth one dial at a time around the leaders, proposes the deepest, refines it by single-dial moves, looks beyond a grid end the depth runs into, and across the designs reads the edge first and then the depth; the trigger's arrival is its event's alone, as the live trigger reads it, so no dial feeds it. The trades are scored the way the live record is: target first or stop first on closes from the fill, against the break-even the plan needed and the calibrated bar its own paths set, after costs, in blocks of 63 sessions. A result is counted in multiples of the risk: for a plan bought at the close, the fill's distance to its stop, and for the stepped plan, which is bought where a close first sits in its zone and so anywhere down to its stop, the distance its plan stated, a fill nearer its stop than the stop setting's floor being no trade; a trade that runs out of sessions is counted at its last close, as its benchmark is, and never as a win; and each record the page states is stated again without its largest results by size (see: The stepped plan's result is counted on the risk its plan stated, and a fill nearer its stop than the stop setting's floor is no trade). The report is one page, every figure on it history, in seven parts: the starting point in plain words with how it differs from the live rule, the variants with their evidence, the seven conditions kept or dropped and why, the strongest candidates beside the live rule year by year on the edge and the raw average with the trades before and after one open trade a stock, the plateau maps on the edge, what was read as it stands today with the missing departures and a stop not at a band flagged, and the point-in-time result with the machine time, the decisions the run took itself and what failed, and last the registration command the freeze would use, not run. Each run writes the page in a folder of its own beside the store, and the read surface serves the newest on its own route with the earlier runs linked.

The sweep history reads the live store directly and writes nothing to it (see: The sweep reads the live store read-only in short reads and writes nothing to it, pausing for every night), and the surprises the earnings beat reads come from a pull of their own the operator runs (see: The surprises pulled before the store's year sit beside the pulled prints and are read by no night). Nothing the sweep computes is registered: the freeze that registers the starting point and its variants at one instant, retiring the six standing today, is a separate command taken on the operator's word, and every checkpoint judges only the trades after it (see: The variations a sweep explores are exploration, and count toward no correction of the live family).

Each setup family has a sweep of its own, run by hand for one family at a time, in minutes, since a family's grid holds tens of settings and not millions (see: A setup family's sweep replays its own rule over the stored history and proposes the best edge among the settings meeting its floors, or brings the strongest where none does). It reads the history the sweep history reads and replays the family's own rule over every scored session at each setting of the grid section 17 states for it, the market check at the live filter's floor closing every list together, walking the nights in order as the page lists them, in the family's own order with its names a night and one open trade a stock, each trade bought at the close under the family's own exit and read as an edge over the same plan entered on every member that night. A setting's record is its trades with a result, the nights a stock was listed, its edge and plain result in multiples of the risk with the edge's standard error, each year's edge, the recent years together and the edge without its largest results by size; the proposal and its variants are held to section 17's floors, and a family no setting of which meets them proposes nothing and keeps its provisional settings and its picks, its report bringing the operator the five strongest settings and what could be tried next (see: No family on any index is set aside or hidden by a test result without the operator's word). The report states the test the family's checkpoints read from its freeze before anything is frozen, and is written in a run folder of its own beside the pullback sweep's runs, served on the same route. Nothing is registered: each family's freeze is the operator's.

The operator froze the four on 2026-10-02 after reading the reports. The pullback freezes at its base, the open filter version's settings with the reward-to-risk floor section 17 states, opened as the next version by the shape command, which retires the swing family and registers it again for that version at the same instant (see: The pullback's freeze opens its base as the next filter version and registers the swing family again at one instant). The breakouts and the earnings drift freeze at their sweeps' proposals, each proposal checked first against its one-step neighbours, two of each one's five meeting the floors, so neither is a point the history happened to favour; the register command writes each family's live rule, those neighbours and the operator's own variants at one instant, the breakout's provisional setting and the drift's proposal with a wider stop (see: The new families freeze at their sweeps' proposals, the breakout's provisional setting and the drift's wider stop registered beside them as variants). The sector leaders' one qualifying setting has no qualifying neighbour, and it is registered as the pullback's variant rather than frozen as a family (see: The sector leaders are a variant of the pullback's starting point and not a family of their own). From the freeze each registered family rule is evaluated every night at its own settings, keeps its own list of at most five a night with one open trade a stock, and stores each trade with its result in multiples of its risk and the benchmark of the same plan on every member that night, and the run page reads each rule's record over its own trades in the blocks and looks section 13.6 states (see: A registered family rule is evaluated every night at its own settings and keeps its own list, its trades stored with their benchmark when they end).

The ideas' run, run by hand once the freezes were taken and in minutes, tests kinds of idea the sweep's grid does not hold, each added to the pullback's base alone (see: A new idea is added to the base one at a time and kept only where it is better in six of eight years). The base is today's rule with its reward-to-risk floor raised, the setting the pullback froze at, and today's rule before the freeze stands beside every figure (see: The base is today's rule with a reward-to-risk floor of 2 until the ideas' run says otherwise). It reads the sweep's candidates over the history the sweep history reads, with the index's and the VIX's daily series the operator pulled (see: The index's and the VIX's daily series are pulled beside the pulled bars, marked by their pull and read by no night), and walks the live design night by night with one open trade a stock. Section 17's rows state the ideas and the test: market switches read on the listing session's close, a stop touched inside the day, the night's best few, a trailing stop, a stop no closer than a typical move, and the base's own exit held for less. A market switch is judged on the year's total result, since the edge subtracts what every member made that night, so keeping off a falling market lowers the benchmark with the trades (see: A market switch is judged on the year's total result, since the edge subtracts what every member made that night). The ideas that pass are combined into a starting point, and the report states it beside today's rule and the base with its variants, each idea with its evidence and its answers, the ideas tried against what luck alone would pass, and the registration a freeze would use. Nothing it finds is registered: a starting point it proposes is a freeze of its own, taken on the operator's word.

The same ideas are read on the breakouts and the earnings drift as frozen, by hand and one family a run, on the operator's ruling of 2026-10-02 (see: The frozen families are read with the pullback's ideas one at a time, and nothing they show is frozen or registered). Each family's base is its live rule at the setting it froze at, replayed over the history its sweep reads as its sweep walks it, and each idea that fits the family is added to it alone and judged by the pullback's test: the six market switches, the stop touched inside the day, a stop no closer than a typical move, the night's best three and the family's own exit held for less, and for the drift alone, whose plan has a target where the breakout's already trails, the two trailing stops. Each new exit's benchmark is the same plan on every member that night under that exit. The report states each family's tries, its passes and what luck alone would pass of that many, and says where an idea changes nothing the rule makes. Nothing it shows is frozen or registered.

From the reports of that run the operator ruled on 2026-10-03 that two of its market switches be registered as variants, the breakout's live rule listing only on nights the index closes above its 200-session average and the drift's only on nights the VIX closes under its close ten sessions before, each the live rule at its frozen settings with that switch and nothing else moved (see: The breakout and the earnings drift each register a variant listing only on nights its market switch is open, each family registered again whole and its records replayed). A switch is a setting every registration of the two families states, nought where it holds none, read after the family's own gates as a gate of its own and closed on a night its closes do not reach. Adding it moves both families' evaluators, so each family is registered again whole at one instant, its seven rules under their names and settings and the switched variant beside them. Where each rule's record counts from is read by the replay a registration runs before it writes: where the replay reproduces every trade the rule's record stored, its record carries on from where it began, and otherwise it counts from the first session after the registration (see: A family rule registered again keeps its record from its first registration where a replay of its stored nights reproduces every trade, and restarts at the change otherwise). The night asks for the index's and the VIX's daily series once each to read the switches (see: The night asks for the market series' daily closes once a series, and keeps them apart from the members' bars).

The context checks are read on the frozen families in one run by hand, each added alone to its family as frozen and judged against it, and nothing they show is frozen or registered (see: The context checks are read on the frozen families one at a time, and nothing they show is frozen or registered). The earnings drift reads its print's revenue growth twice: as a filter keeping a print whose quarter's revenue grew on the same quarter a year before, and as an order keeping the night's first three with the largest growth first. A print's growth is its quarter's revenue as first filed against the same quarter's a year before, its quarter the newest its filer states ending within a stated span before the report, both read whatever day they were first filed, with the share of each idea's trades reading one filed after their buy stated beside its figures (see: A drift print's revenue growth is its quarter's revenue as first filed against the same quarter a year before). The drift's ideas are judged by the year tests, the test without the five largest and the trade floor, with no floor of nights, since the drift lists only after a strong reported beat and leaves most nights empty (see: The drift's context ideas are judged by the year tests, the test without the five largest and a thousand trades with no floor of nights). The pullback reads one order, the night's first three with the furthest fall of its RSI from its high session to the night first, judged by the pullback's own test against its base, the base's first three in the list's own order standing beside it (see: The pullback's RSI-fall order keeps the night's first three by how far its RSI fell from its high session). No news is read, the provider's sentiment not being shown to be a fixed word list's score (see: Six context checks are not adopted, each for the reason it states). Evidence: Jegadeesh and Livnat (2006) find an earnings surprise backed by a revenue surprise drifts further than one that is not; Sloan (1996) finds earnings made of accruals persist less than earnings made of cash, so a beat with no growth in the revenue beneath it is the kind least likely to last. Judgement: the RSI's fall as an order, which no study sets, read because the brief asks for it to be tested against the list's own order, and the three kept, the count the ideas' run passed.

The sector heavyweights have a sweep of their own, run by hand through the family sweep's command, which walks a book rather than a night's list since the family rotates on its rebalances (see: The heavyweights' sweep replays the book over the pulled history across its settings and proposes the best edge among those meeting the family sweeps' floors). It reads the history the sweep history reads with the companies, share counts, splits and sector funds the history pull stored, values every member on each session a rebalance reads as it stood, and reads each sector's largest companies, leads and leaders by the night's own rule at each setting section 17 states for it, a fund's return in the members' mean's place or a beta of at least one where a setting reads it (see: The sector heavyweights hold the largest companies leading their sectors, rotated on the first session of each month whose stored year holds the closes their readings need). It walks the holdings session by session as the book walks them, one holding a stock, and scores each by its return in percent less the equal-weighted return of the size cut it was chosen from, every member's and the index's returns beside it as context (see: A sector heavyweight's trade is scored by its percent return less the equal-weighted return of the size cut it was chosen from). A holding counts in the year it was sold in, and one still held at the history's end in none. The proposal is held to the family sweeps' floors, and the report states every setting one step from it and what luck alone would put above nothing in as many years, and holds the replay at the setting the family froze at, which the night's book holds at, to every rebalance the night's book stored, naming each sector it reads differently. Nothing is registered by the sweep: the family froze at its proposal on the operator's go (see: The sector heavyweights freeze at their sweep's proposal, the proposal's three passing neighbours registered beside them as variants).

The S&P 1500 is tested first on today's members, by a run of its own started by hand (see: A wider universe is tested first on today's members, and widened only where a family's edge improves even so and holds on membership as it stood). The S&P 400's and 600's fundamentals answers list today's members and no span of membership, so a members pull stores each index's members today and the history pull's own pulls, given that index, store their bars, earnings prints, surprises and splits beside the S&P 500's, each read by no night. The sweep history reads the 1,500 as the S&P 500's history as stored with those members beside it, each a member on every session, and the run replays each swing family's rule as frozen, the pullback's base, the breakout and the earnings drift, over the 1,500 and over the 500 alone, judging the 1,500 against the 500 by the test the ideas' run judges an idea by, on the edge, with what luck alone passes over its three tries. A history of today's members holds the companies that stayed in or grew into the indices and none that fell out or failed, which flatters the wider universe, so every figure the run states for the 1,500 says it holds survivors only. Where no family's edge improves even so the widening is dropped, and where one improves nothing is adopted until the result holds on membership as it stood.

The first test found no family's S&P 500 rule as frozen doing better over the 1,500 than over the 500, and the operator ruled that this shows the 500's settings do not carry to mid and small companies, and not that the S&P 400 and 600 cannot give good picks (see: The S&P 400 and 600 join the universe with rules of their own, since the first test showed only that the 500's settings do not carry to them). So each family is swept on each of the two indices as a rule of its own, its strength ranked, its market check read and its edge measured among that index's members, every result read after the cost a trade pays for its company's size and price (see: A 400 or 600 trade pays the published effective spread for its size and price, and its pass tests read the edge after it), and every figure labelled as read on membership as it stood or on survivors only. Membership as it stood is rebuilt from the quarter-end holdings the S&P 400's and 600's funds file with the SEC, the public filings from the quarter to 2019-09-30 and before them the N-Q for the quarter to 2018-12-31 and the annual report for the year to 2019-03-31, whose schedules name each holding with no identifier, each holding matched to the provider's code by its ISIN and then by its name, a name match kept only where its code traded at the quarter's end at the fund's value a share, every code kept only where its closes move in step with the fund's values a share from one quarter end to the next and a name's at the level at each of them or at one ratio across them, a company renamed since matched to the code its fund held by ISIN within a year and never to one it held beside it, a schedule's holding filed with no identifier carrying the code the next coded quarter's identical name matched, and a name a member from the first snapshot holding it to the last (see: Membership as it stood is rebuilt from the funds' quarterly holdings filed with the SEC, matched by ISIN and then by name) (see: A holding matched by name is kept only where its code traded at the quarter's end) (see: The funds' holdings before their first public N-PORT are read from their N-Q of 2018-12-31 and their annual report of 2019-03-31) (see: A holding's code is kept only where its closes move in step with the fund's values a share, and a match by name is held to the level at each quarter end as well) (see: A code the fund held by ISIN beside a holding at one quarter end is another holding and never that holding renamed) (see: A holding of a schedule filed with no identifier carries the code the next coded quarter's holding of the identical name matched, where the closes move in step across them) (see: A renamed company is matched to a code its fund held by ISIN within a year where its close equals the value a share to the cent at two quarter ends). The sector heavyweights are swept on each index in two designs, the stronger kept (see: The 400 and 600 each sweep two heavyweight designs and keep the stronger after costs), and a family no setting of which passes on an index keeps listing there on its provisional settings until the operator rules (see: No family on any index is set aside or hidden by a test result without the operator's word).

Each sweep run states its answer beside its report in its own folder: passed where its proposal, or a setting its second stage crossed, meets the floors of at least 300 trades and an edge above nothing in 6 of the 8 years after costs, and none passed otherwise, the pullback's base on an index, which searches nothing, stating none. The operator records a run's answer in the store with the worker's sweep-answer command, which refuses a run stating no answer, an index no page reads and a family no card draws, writing nothing for any of them. A family's card on any index then says its sweep found no setting that passed the floors where the newest answer recorded for each of its designs says none passed, the sector heavyweights sweeping two, and no freeze of the family on that index came after it, and goes on listing its picks; the line goes with a newer answer that passes or a freeze registered after it (see: A sweep passes where a setting it read meets the floors, and a card says none passed only where every design's newest answer does).

Five searches of the S&P 400's and 600's families were run once by hand in phase 17's first checkpoint, each read-only on the pulled history as it stood and after costs, each report stating its figures by year, the luck figure for its tries and what could be tried next, and nothing frozen from any of them (see: No family on any index is set aside or hidden by a test result without the operator's word). The S&P 400's drift adds to its second stage a hold of 10 sessions, a surprise of at least 5 or 10 per cent, its print's revenue growth as first filed and known from the report (see: A drift print's revenue growth is its quarter's revenue as first filed against the same quarter a year before), the other index's fund against SPY, and an entry on the first pullback after the reaction, and passes only where a setting's edge over the history's last two years together stands above nothing beside the floors (see: The S&P 400's drift passes a search only where its edge over 2025 and 2026 together stands above nothing). The breakouts on both indices add the breakout day's close in the top quarter of its range and an entry on the first pullback to the level broken (see: The S&P 400's and 600's breakouts and drift read an entry on the first pullback within ten sessions as a level of their second stage). The S&P 400's pullback with profit and cover is read at half steps about the setting the brief names, each neighbour that falls under the floors named with its dial, and its trades replayed under three exits, the stop fixed, moved to the buy or trailing (see: The S&P 400 pullback with profit and cover is read at half steps about the setting the brief names and its trades under three exits); the two indices' pullbacks are searched together and confirmed on each alone (see: The S&P 400's and 600's pullbacks are searched together for a shared setting and confirmed on each alone); and the S&P 600's search looks a second time beyond a grid end and prints the dial binding each setting's depth (see: An index's pullback search looks a second time beyond a grid end and names the dial that binds its depth). The sector heavyweights are read over six settings a design registered in a ruling entry before the run, each with its evidence, and only those, so luck alone passes about one of them (see: The S&P 400's and 600's sector heavyweights are searched over six settings a design registered before the run). Every pull a search needs states its provider calls before it runs, and a pull that would take the day's count past the operator's cap of 5,000 weighted calls stops and asks (see: Every pull states its provider calls before it runs and stops for the operator at the day's cap).

13.10 The setup ledger

Everything above judges the rules by what they picked. Phase 17 adds a record of what they could have picked: the setup ledger, written each night from 17.3 and built over the pulled history by hand, holding every member-session a family's loose gates pass on each of the three indices, the pullback's, the breakout's and the drift's, with the live rule's own pass and the night's list beside it, so what the rule chose and what it passed over sit on the same row (see: A setup is every member-session a family's loose gates pass, and its readings are defined once and read as they stood). The loose gates are each a grid step beyond the widest level any sweep or search tried, stated in section 17, so an engine reading the ledger can place a boundary outside the searched range and find the setups beyond it already there.

A setup stores its anchor rather than its path: the session, the buy at the close, the stop, the target or the trail's distance, and the sessions the trade is given, with the stop's distance in the member's typical moves. Any exit, for the setup or for the benchmark, replays from bars through one function in the core, and the bars the fetcher drops are kept in a table of their own so a path older than the bar store's year still replays (see: The bars the fetcher drops are kept in a table of their own that no night reads, and a setup is stored as its anchor). The benchmark is the same plan, in typical moves, entered at the close on every member of the index that session, and a setup's edge is its result less the benchmark; the benchmark is settled only once every member's path has ended, so an edge is never read against a mean of the members that happened to end first. On the night the setup's cost is stored beside it, the member's own round trip in risks, and the edge after cost beside the edge.

Every reading is defined once, in the core's catalogue, and read as it stood: the forty-five readings of the stock, its business and the market, from the bars to the session, the market series to the session's day and the quarters filed before it, each through the rules' own functions or a ratio over the series' own figures. A reading the inputs do not reach is stored as none and never nought. The night's step appends tonight's setups after the families have drawn every index's list and closes the windows of the setups stored before as their paths end; the build by hand writes the history one index at a time over the pulled bars merged with the store's on membership as it stood, a quarter of sessions a transaction, from a clean copy of the main checkout's own commit as the night is built and refused off main the same way (see: Each night is built from a clean copy of the main checkout's own commit and never from its working tree, and refuses only a checkout off main or ahead of the remote's main), waiting for the night and holding the drain's lock, which the store's copy holds too, while it writes each chunk, and going on from the sessions it has not written, a span written again only when asked. The point-in-time check by hand takes a seeded sample of each year's history setups and rebuilds each one's readings from the history cut at its own session, holding only what stood then, the earnings calendar kept whole since a report's date is announced before it; a reading that read past its session differs, and is named. The history it cuts is read through the session the build read it through, since the years the pull holds before the store's are priced by the median ratio of the two over the sessions both hold to that end, and a history read to another end prices them a rounding apart; and a swing setup's own readings, its plan's reward to risk, its freshness, its band's strength, its volume multiple, its range ratio and its reaction, are rebuilt by its family's own gates over the cut, a setup those gates do not pass there named as one. The vocabulary the loop's later sections use is this section's: a setup, its anchor, its plan, its benchmark, its edge, and the ledger that holds them.

Five of the readings are the business's, read from the SEC's facts as first filed and only from those filed before the setup's session: the newest quarter's revenue against the same quarter's a year before, how far that growth moved from the quarter before's, the gross and the operating margin against the same quarter's a year before, and the newest fiscal year's cash from operations over its net income (see: The SEC's facts are stored as first filed in a table the night reads, and a setup's business readings read those filed before its session). The facts are kept fresh by the night's filings refresh after the close, which reads the archive's daily index for the days since it last read one and asks the archive for the facts of the members that filed a report, an amendment or a results announcement, and of no other; once it has stored them the ledger reads the business readings of the night's setups again for those members, so a night's row reads every filing the archive posted before its session, as a row the history writes does (see: The night refreshes the facts of the members that filed since its last read of the archive's daily index, after the close under its own limit). The whole refresh by hand asks every filer the store knows once, and the monthly run repeats it as the catch-all.

The S&P 500's heavyweights add a fourth family: on each rebalance of the book, each member of each sector's size cut, its ten largest companies by value as they stood, is a setup bought at the session's close, the book's buys passed and picked. The rule places no stop, so each is held as the rule holds a stock it bought, to the first later rebalance at which the rule does not buy it and never past a year's sessions, and its result is a fraction of the buy against its size cut over the same sessions, as the book scores a holding (see: A heavyweights' setup is each member of its sector's size cut on a rebalance of the S&P 500's book, held as the rule holds a buy) (see: A sector heavyweight's trade is scored by its percent return less the equal-weighted return of the size cut it was chosen from). The night reads the size cut the book stored; the history build reads the same rebalances by the heavyweights' sweep's own replay. The S&P 400's and 600's heavyweights are provisional and their books store no size cut, so they add no setup until a freeze registers their live rule.

13.11 The loop's nightly half

The loop learns from the ledger, and the ledger is written by the night. Each evening the families draw their lists, the ledger appends every near-setup those lists passed over beside the ones they took, and the windows of the setups stored before close as their paths end. After the close the filings refresh stores the facts of the members that filed, the ledger reads the business readings of the night's setups again from them, and the summary the Ledger page draws is rewritten. Nothing in this half proposes or changes a rule: it records, and the monthly half reads what it recorded (see: A setup is every member-session a family's loose gates pass, and its readings are defined once and read as they stood).

Key. Read it downward, one night. A box with a green edge on its left is arithmetic the night runs, and a box with a blue rule across its top is a store the night writes. The box with the source colour is the one step that reads from outside: the SEC's archive, read after the close for the members that filed and for no other.

The top three run inside the night's arithmetic; the bottom three run after its close, so a slow archive delays none of the lists. No box proposes, tests or changes a rule; the monthly half does that, from what these rows recorded.

13.12 The walk-forward tester

A change to a rule is judged only on years the change never saw. The tester holds a fold a year, from 2022 to the year of the newest session, the newest a partial year of the months since the latest complete one. Each fold learns on what ended before its year's first session and is tested on what was entered in its year, so a trade or a setup still open on that session is learned on by none of the folds it reaches into: the purge is by its actual end and not by a fixed gap, which keeps more of the last learning months (see: A change is adopted only on test years the proposal never saw, and a search is judged as a procedure run year by year). What a proposal is built from is handed to it as a view cut at the fold's first session, holding only what ended before it, and a read of that session or any later one is refused and named, so nothing built in a fold can have read the year it is tested on.

A search is judged as a procedure. Part 0's searches with a set of tries, the breakout's and the drift's grids on the S&P 400 and 600, the drift at the stop floor its runbook names and on the S&P 400 with its last two learning years read, and the sector heavyweights' six settings in each design, are run inside every fold: each setting is walked once over the whole history, since a walk's trades before a session are the same whatever comes after it, and a fold reads only the trades that ended before its year through its view and chooses as the search chooses, with the family floors in proportion to the years it learns on (see: A search run inside a fold reads the family floors in proportion to the years it learns on). The choice is scored on the fold's year against the index's current rule, both walked by the same walk; a fold whose years before meet no setting's floors tests the rule today against itself, and that year adds nothing either way. The pullback's searches are budgeted by the clock rather than by a set of tries, so a fold would read a different set of settings on another machine, and they are not run inside a fold; the pullback's first proposals come from the engines. What is put forward is the procedure run on all finished data, with how many folds chose within a grid step of it.

The comparison is the paired difference in total edge after costs: each trade's edge after its round trip, the proposal's trades against the rule's, summed over blocks of 63 sessions keyed on the session each was entered on from the test span's first, a block read once its whole outcome window has closed (see: A proposal passes the tester on a block sign-flip test of its total edge after costs against the current rule, corrected within a run and held to a fixed bar across runs). The heavyweights' unit is a book's month, from the close of the session one month opens on to the close of the next month's, its edge the mean over the holdings held across any part of it of each holding's return less its size cut's over the sessions it held, a holding paying its round trip in the month it was bought (see: A sector heavyweights book is judged a month at a time, each month's edge the mean over the holdings it held). The blocks' sums are studentised as a candidate's record is and read against every arrangement of their signs, a fixed seed's draws standing in past twenty-four blocks; the proposals tested for one rule in a run are read together by Romano and Wolf's step-down, one sign vector applied to all of them at once, and a proposal's gate holds at an adjusted p-value of 0.05 over 12 or under, over at least eight blocks. Beside it stand three screens, each read on its own: better in at least three in five of the complete test years holding 50 trades or a book's twelve months a side, the latest complete year counted and better; still above nothing with the five largest results by size left out of each side; and at least 300 test trades for a swing family or 36 months for a book. A proposal passes where all four hold and it names a change; the difference the gate would detect four times in five at the bar is read from the blocks' own scatter and drawn beside it, since a test that cannot detect the edges the rules carry passes nothing and says nothing either way. The rule today was itself chosen on these test years, so a proposal reads understated against it, and the Loop page says so.

Key. Read it a row at a time; each row is a fold. The bar with the green edge is what the fold learns on: every trade and setup that ended before the fold's year began, from the history's first scored year. The shaded bar after it is the year the fold is tested on, every trade entered in it, the proposal's against the rule's. The last row's dashed bar is the months since the latest complete year: it is tested and drawn, and the stability screen does not count it.

Nothing crosses a row's cut. A trade still open on the year's first session is in none of the row's learning, and the view a proposal is built from refuses any read of that session or a later one; the setting a row chooses is scored on its own year alone.

13.13 The trade autopsy, winners against losers and the engines' hooks

The monthly half reads what the nightly half recorded and proposes, and the tester judges each proposal on the years it never saw, one family on one index at a time (see: Each family on each index is proposed for, tested on and approved separately, on its own index's history alone). Its first engine is the trade autopsy. For each family on each index it reads what the rule's own finished trades did between their buy and their end, from their closes: the median trade's best close and its worst, in risks; the sessions from the buy to the best close; how many of the trades the stop ended had first closed a risk up; and how far under the buy the trades the target ended fell first. The figures are read over the whole history and are context, never a test: they say why an exit might help, and the years a proposal never saw say whether it did (see: The trade autopsy proposes exits of a fixed menu, each tested as the procedure that chose it).

The autopsy proposes from a menu fixed before any trade is read, its figures stated in section 17. For the swing families: the stop raised to the buy once a close is a number of risks up; a trail of a number of typical moves under the highest close, from the buy or once a close is a number of risks up, with no target; a fixed target in risks; a sale at the close a number of sessions in unless the trade is above the buy or half a risk up; and half sold at the target with the rest trailed. For the sector heavyweights: a holding also sold at a close under its 200-day average, and the book rebalanced each week, each through the book's own walk. Each exit changes only what it names and keeps the rest of the plan, its stop, its cap and its target or its trail, and is replayed exactly on the closes from the setup's anchor, a close under the stop selling at that close, through one function in the core that a rule's walk on the night and the tester share; its benchmark is the same plan under the same exit entered at the close on every member that session.

Each exit is tested as the procedure that chose it. The rule is walked once over the whole history under its own exit and once under each of the menu's, each trade after its round trip; each fold ranks the exits whose edge on what ended before its year stands above the rule's own and meets the family floors in proportion to the years it learns on, and the k-th proposal is the k-th exit each fold ranks, scored on the fold's year against the rule, at most five a family an index (see: A search run inside a fold reads the family floors in proportion to the years it learns on). A proposal is named by the k-th exit on all finished data, with its finding in words beside it: the autopsy's figures and the exit's edge on the years it learned on against the rule's. The breakout and the drift are walked on every index, the S&P 400's and 600's provisional pullback as its record replays it, and the heavyweights' two on every index with a book's month as their unit; the S&P 500's pullback is the swing filter's walk and is proposed no exit.

The second engine sets winners against losers. Over the same families on the same indices it reads every listing the rule makes over the history, kept by the rule or not, with its edge after its round trip had it been taken and the ledger's readings of it on its session, read through the catalogue's own function as the night reads them for a rule's hooks. Each fold searches the listings that ended before its year: each reading cut at its deciles, the tenth to the ninth, either side, a condition keeping at least the family floor in proportion to the fold's learning years and fewer than every listing holding the reading, scored by the mean edge of the listings it keeps; and beneath the strongest of them its pair, the best second condition on another reading over the listings the first keeps, the greedy tree's second level. A condition goes forward only where its score stands above the rule's own mean and above the 95th percentile of a null that shuffles which listing carries which edge within each night and reads the search's best again on each arrangement: every arrangement where the nights hold no more than 199 of them, and otherwise 199 drawn at a fixed seed (see: Winners against losers proposes a condition only where it beats a within-night shuffle of its own search). A shuffle within a night keeps what the market did that night and breaks only which of its listings a reading points at, so a reading that only tells one night from another, the market's own level among them, passes no null. The k-th proposal is the k-th condition each fold keeps, the rule walked with it over the fold's year against the rule as it stands, at most five a family an index, each stated as the conditions a rule's hooks read. Each reading's spread over every finished listing is stored beside the proposals, the winners' and the losers' medians and the mean edge of each tenth in the reading's order, and the Loop page draws it.

What a proposal changes is a setting the rule's walk already reads, so an approval changes stored settings and never code (see: Every engine's settings hooks land together and all default off, so the families' pins move once). A registered family rule may state beside its own parameters the exit of the menu its trades are walked under, conditions on the ledger's readings that a member passing its own gates must also meet, and a score over those readings that its list is ordered by, with the least score kept. A rule stating none is listed, walked and benchmarked exactly as before the hooks existed, and no rule standing states one. The hooks are pinned by the S&P 500's breakout and drift rules and by every S&P 400 and 600 rule, so they moved those pins once, and the S&P 500's rules were registered again with a replay that keeps each record where every trade is reproduced. A rule whose hooks read readings is handed the night's from the ledger's own catalogue on every index, and lists nothing on a night that supplies none; a heavyweights book's exits are its own settings, and a hook stated beside its parameters is refused.

Key. Read it downward, one month. The blue-topped box is what the nightly half stored: the ledger's setups and each rule's own trades. Green boxes compute: the engines propose, the tester judges each proposal against the rule today on the years the proposal never saw, and an approved change is applied as a stored setting by the worker before the next night. Teal boxes serve pages: the Loop page draws what the tester stored and computes nothing. Orange boxes are things outside the system, here the operator.

Nothing reaches the bottom box without the operator's approval, and a declined proposal changes nothing. The autopsy is the engine built first; the conditions and the score propose through the same boxes, each a setting the rule's walk already reads.

Key. Illustrative: the path is drawn to show what is read and not any stock's trade. The heavy line is the trade's closes from its buy.
