21. Decisions

The decisions and the superseded ones live in the decisions record kept beside this document, grouped by topic, and not here. A decision stated in this document and again in a register is two places holding one fact, and one of them always loses.

Every rule in this document that a later session could reasonably choose differently, where the wrong choice would be invisible, is a named decision in that record. This document cites them by their exact name, in the form (see: Code owns every number), and the check named decision-resolves asserts that every citation matches a bold name in the record and that no two decisions share a name. The check named no-superseded-citation asserts that no citation resolves to a name under Previously decided.

Cite the name, never a number. A misremembered name fails to resolve; a misremembered number resolves to the wrong decision and nobody notices.

22. Open questions

The questions phase 10 leaves open are listed first, each linked from the rule that rests on it. Before phase 10 no question was open. Every fork that stood here has been settled, and each is recorded below with how it settled rather than deleted. The six that stood here on 4 September were not questions: three were values with a stated way of settling them, which now sit in the limits table and the phase table; two were things already decided elsewhere in this document; and one was a recommendation written as a question. They are recorded in section 22 and the changelog rather than left here, because an open list that holds settled things makes the one real fork harder to see.

Open questions

QuestionWhy it is open
Whether the six live reasons' verdict should take the block sign-flip testThe live family is judged by a Poisson-binomial test that assumes independent setups, built at phase 8 and unchanged by phase 10. The operator's to rule.
Whether the live family should count a setup entered and stopped in one sessionIts verdict drops them for want of a break-even; 8 of 254 stored losses take that shape. The operator's to rule.
Whether band strength or the plan's reward to risk breaks a tie betterResearch points both ways; the three orders are compared on the run page against the old order as the benchmark.
How many nights a new trend label must hold before it restores buying zonesNo study was found; 2 is proposed and settled from how often a label returns, a changed count being a new version.
How far past an edge a close must sit for a crossing to countNo study found sets the margin. The operator settled it at 0.5 of a typical move on 2026-09-22, on per-night counts alone, and changing it is a new registration rather than an edit.
Whether dependence between setups runs longer than 63 sessions through a market regimeThe block length rests on the outcome window, and a regime lasting longer would leave blocks correlated.
Whether the block should be a multiple of the outcome window rather than equal to itNo study read settles the multiple, and the registered length is never shortened by the data.
Whether an always-valid test exists under this clustering that could be read every nightAlways-valid designs are read continuously, and none read here covers setups clustered in blocks of shared bars.
What the closing auction costs an S&P 500 nameThe costs read are spreads and institutional round trips, not the auction a close fill assumes.
Whether a price level predicts anything at allThe premise the bands, the tranches and the six reasons all rest on, and the studies read answer it three ways. Park and Irwin find most of the modern literature positive and most of it carrying data snooping, rules picked after the fact and weak treatment of risk and costs; Osler finds published levels bounced more often than arbitrary ones while their published strength ratings bore no consistent relation to bouncing; Chung and Bellotti find a level's prior bounces do bear on whether it holds. The candidates' own records are what answer it here, and none has been registered.

Settled questions

Was askedHow it settled
Which of two hand-written reports was right about a moving averageNot a question once the specification moved inside this document. Every number in a report is computed from stored bars under the decision named Code owns every number, and fixture expectations are derived from the rules rather than from any report, so there is nothing left to reconcile.
The project's nameEquityBrief, confirmed 4 September.
Where transcripts come fromNowhere that is bought. See the decision named Transcripts are opportunistic, never a dependency. The question should not have been written, because the source map already showed the press release carrying what the report needs.
The news-jump multipleSet in the limits table: at least five articles in five sessions and at least three times the name's own trailing median.
The volume shelf thresholdSet in the limits table at twice an even share, with phase 3 widening the fixture to four names so the number is checked before anything depends on it.
A directional scoreSettled 5 September in a narrower form than asked. Bucket-shaped conditions are registered and scored like any other candidate, so the data improves which reasons fire rather than producing a separate ranking. A reason's measured record is displayed beside the reason under section 15.5, which is the visible half of what was wanted. What is not built is a number beside each ticker, because separating small edges needs years of setups this list cannot produce and such a number would be read as a probability of making money.
Where theme material comes fromA search tool called inside the research loop, with a key already in hand and two trial searches run against it. See the decision named Theme material comes from a search tool, and per-name material never does, whose results are stored like any other document. This row named half of it until 6.0, and a name given in half is the paraphrase the citation rule exists to reject. It should not have stayed on this list after the key was set up.
Whether the watch list is pre-warmedSettled twice. On 4 September the answer was no, because anticipation meant spending money on names that might not be opened. On 5 September that reasoning stopped applying, because research can now be written locally at no cost, so the overnight queue writes free drafts for every name and the paid model stays strictly on demand. The superseded decision and its original reasoning are in section 22.
